title: DEP: Native System One endpoint (`/v1/systemone`)
body:
## Summary

This DEP adds `POST /v1/systemone` to the Dynamo frontend. The route implements the TypeSafe/Jev wire protocol, where a client asks `noul`, `choice` and `score` questions about a state and gets probabilities back instead of generated text.

The scope is the generative readout, which works with any chat model Dynamo already serves. The handler renders the state once, then scores each question as a one-token completion over the shared token prefix, using `logprob_token_ids`. The vLLM backend supports this today without engine changes.

The design copies the behavior of SGLang's merged `/v1/systemone` route ([SGLang PR 41208](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41208)): same prompt, labels, scoring, confidence and response. A client should get the same answers from either server. What Dynamo adds is placement across replicas, so all the questions of a request land on the worker holding the state prefix, and one route that works over several backends.

## Motivation

A System One model answers structured questions about a state with calibrated probabilities. Each question costs one prefill and one scored token, with no decode loop. The TypeSafe/Jev HTTP API has become the common interface for these models and the official SDKs target it. Today the options for serving it are side-car wrappers (openjev-sglang, AnyJev used as a library), SGLang's single-engine route, or the closed Jev API.

Dynamo already has most of the pieces:

- The frontend enables routes per model type. `POST /v1/classify` and `/v1/pooling` are registered in `get_endpoints_router` and switched on through `state.flags` when a worker of that type registers. `/v1/systemone` can follow the same pattern.
- `logprob_token_ids` already flows from the request allowlist through the preprocessor to vLLM's sampling params, so the vLLM path needs no engine change.
- The KV-aware router can place the state prefix on one worker, and worker pinning can keep the rest of the request there. A single-engine route or a side-car cannot do this across replicas.

Current support across the ecosystem (checked September 2026):

| Project | System One support |
|---|---|
| TypeSafe / Jev (`api.typesafe.ai`) | Closed reference model, defines the wire protocol |
| vLLM | No built-in endpoint. [vLLM PR 57250](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57250) (DiffusionGemma structured reads, merged 2026-09-22) includes an example `/v1/systemone` proxy. [vLLM PR 57417](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57417) and [vLLM PR 58216](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58216) (merged) make DiffusionGemma honor `logprob_token_ids`. [vLLM PR 58429](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58429) (Laya typed-decision models) is open. Maintainers are discussing a built-in endpoint but there is no public proposal yet. The existing `/generative_scoring` route scores `label_token_ids` in one step. |
| SGLang | Built-in `/v1/systemone` ([SGLang PR 41208](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41208), merged 2026-09-25), built on the candidate scoring from [SGLang PR 40826](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40826). The earlier `/v1/decisions` proposal ([SGLang PR 40992](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40992)) was closed and merged into it. There is also the standalone `ekzhang/openjev-sglang` wrapper. |
| AnyJev (Nokia applied research) | Library: label logprobs, cyclic-shift debiasing, batch-prior calibration |
| Standalone servers | `razorback16/openjev` (DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B on vLLM or MLX, plus Laya and Verdict encoders), `yijunyu/jev-rs` (Rust, on llama-server or any OpenAI-compatible backend), `TheoLeeCJ/SemIf`, formerly OpenJev (llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU) |
| Dynamo | None today (this DEP) |

## Goals and non-goals

Goals:

1. Serve `/v1/systemone` from the Dynamo frontend.
2. Support any served chat model, with per-backend capability checks.
3. Return the same answers as SGLang's `/v1/systemone` for the same model and chat template, and match TypeSafe's documented examples and the official SDKs.

Non-goals for v1:

- `/permute` and `/separate` (Jev and LocalAI extensions), the `stats` and `assets_used` fields, and streaming.
- System One models that are not chat models (see Future work).

## Wire protocol

```
POST /v1/systemone
{ "model": "<served-model>",
  "state": <string|object|array>,
  "questions": { "<id>": { "type": "noul|choice|score",
                            "instructions": "...",
                            "criteria": ... } } }
```

The three question types:

- `noul` is a yes/no question. `criteria` is optional and can describe each side as `{"true": ..., "false": ...}`. The answer is `noul`, the probability of true, with no `confidence`.
- `choice` takes `criteria` as a map from option name to description (the description can be `null`). The answer has `choice`, `probabilities` keyed by option name, and `confidence`.
- `score` takes `criteria` as an ordered list of levels. The answer has `score` (the expected level index, starting at 0), `legend` and `probabilities` keyed `"0"` to `"L-1"`, and `confidence`.

The response is `{ "model", "answers": { <id>: ... }, "usage": { "input_tokens", "output_tokens" } }`. Validation errors return 422 with FastAPI's `{"detail":[...]}` list. Overload returns 529 with `Retry-After`, which is already Dynamo's default overload status (`DYN_HTTP_OVERLOAD_STATUS_CODE`). The SDKs send a Bearer token, which Dynamo treats as it does for its other routes. The protocol does not define `usage`, so we follow SGLang: `input_tokens` counts every scored prompt and `output_tokens` is 0.

### Confidence

Every implementation we checked computes choice confidence the same way, clamped to [0, 1]. Score confidence has two versions in the wild:

```
choice:           (K * pmax - 1) / (K - 1)
score (adapter):  1 - E|i - mode| / mean|i - (L-1)/2|     # typesafe-ai/system-one-adapter-python
score (alt):      (L * pmax - 1) / (L - 1)                # choice formula applied to levels
```

TypeSafe's docs have one score example (`p = [0, 0.95, 0.05]`), and both formulas give 0.925 on it, so the docs don't decide. They differ on spread-out distributions: `p = [0.5, 0, 0.5]` gives 0 with the adapter formula and 0.25 with the other. We use the adapter formula, floored at 0, as SGLang does. It is TypeSafe's own published code and it takes the order of the levels into account. A question with a single option or level gets confidence 1.

## Design

### Why a core endpoint

The frontend extension hook only supports static GET routes (`frontend_extension.rs`: "Currently only `GET` routes are supported") and can't call engines. So the endpoint follows the pattern of the experimental Anthropic messages API: an off-by-default flag and a handler that translates to the OpenAI protocol internally and calls an existing engine. Here that engine is the completions engine, called with token-ID prompts.

### Files

Paths checked against upstream `main`:

| Change | Location |
|---|---|
| `EndpointType::SystemOne` variant | `lib/llm/src/endpoint_type.rs` |
| Flag `--enable-systemone-api` (`DYN_ENABLE_SYSTEMONE_API`) and path override `DYN_HTTP_SVC_SYSTEMONE_PATH` | `frontend_config.rs`, `components/src/dynamo/frontend/frontend_args.py`, `components/src/dynamo/frontend/main.py` |
| Route registration | `service_v2.rs::get_endpoints_router`, like `anthropic_messages_router` |
| Request and response types, prompt building, scoring | new `lib/llm/src/protocols/systemone/` |
| Handler | new `lib/llm/src/http/service/systemone.rs` |
| Metrics label, OpenAPI doc, docs page | `metrics.rs` (`Endpoint::SystemOne`), `docs/fern/...` |

### Handler

Steps tagged (SGLang) match SGLang's route (`python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/systemone/` and `openai/serving_decisions.py`) so the answers are the same. The other steps are specific to running across several workers.

1. Validate (SGLang). Errors return 422 with FastAPI's detail list, without the `input` echo. A request needs at least one question. Choice questions take 1 to 255 options with distinct names, score questions take 1 to 10 levels, and a noul question needs instructions or a true/false description. Unknown keys inside a question are rejected, because a typo there would silently ask a different question. Unknown top-level fields are ignored, as the published schema allows. The `/v1/decisions` fields that would change answers (`temperature`, `prompt_format_version`, `return_prompt_token_ids`) are rejected by name. Dynamo adds configurable limits of 128 questions, 32,768 tokens per prompt and 65,536 tokens per request. The handler then resolves the model (`resolve_canonical_name`) and gets the completions engine (`ModelManager::get_completions_engine`, `discovery/model_manager.rs:1379`).

2. Build the prompt (SGLang). Each question is one user message containing the state (a string as is, anything else as compact JSON), a blank line, and a question block:
   - choice: `Question: <instructions>`, then one line per option, `A: <name> - <description>` or just `A: <name>`, then `Answer with the letter of one option only.`
   - score: `Question: <instructions>`, then one line per level, `0: <level>`, then `Answer with the number of one level only.`
   - noul: `Is the following true? <instructions>`, then `yes: <true description>` and `no: <false description>` if given, then `Answer with yes or no only.`

   The `Question:` line is left out when `instructions` is blank. The message is rendered with the model card's chat template (`prompt_formatter_from_mdc`, `preprocessor/prompt.rs:381`) with `add_generation_prompt=true` and the template's reasoning toggle set to false. The toggle is found from the configured reasoning parser, as in SGLang. It has to be set explicitly because Dynamo's Anthropic handler enables thinking whenever a reasoning parser is configured. The handler accepts SGLang's `chat_template_kwargs` extension. It returns 400 if a request turns the toggle on, or if the template always opens a reasoning block where the answer should go.

3. Pick labels (SGLang). Noul uses `yes` and `no`, choice uses `A` to `Z`, and score uses `0` to `9`. Above 26 options every option gets a two-letter label (`AA`, `AB`, and so on). Checking hundreds of labels against the full prompt is slow, so this only works when the template puts an added token, such as Qwen's `</think>`, between the message and the answer position. Labels can then be checked against the end of the template alone. Otherwise the request gets a 400. A label is valid only if `encode(prompt + label) == encode(prompt) + [id]` and `id` differs from every other label's ID. The tokenizer comes from the worker's model card (`ModelDeploymentCard::tokenizer()`), and the two-letter label set is cached per model and template.

4. Tokenize the state once. All prompts in a request start with the same template header, state and blank line. The handler renders once with a marker where the question block goes, splits the result into a prefix and an ending, and tokenizes the prefix once. Each branch prompt is the prefix IDs followed by the tokenized question block and ending, sent as a token-ID prompt (`PromptInput::Tokens` is already supported). Tokens can merge across the split, for example when the state ends in newlines. So on each request the handler compares the split tokens of the first question with its whole-prompt tokens, and tokenizes every prompt whole if they differ. This keeps the prompt tokens identical to SGLang's.

5. Place the prefix, then fan out. SGLang scores all questions in one engine call and its radix cache shares the prefix between them. With several replicas, Dynamo has to keep them together itself. It sends the first question alone through the KV-aware router, which computes the shared prefix on one worker. It then sends the remaining questions to that worker with `nvext.backend_instance_id`, because the router's view of the cache lags behind a request that just finished. Each branch uses `max_tokens=1` and `logprob_token_ids=[labels]`. The fan-out reuses the `completions_batch` pattern (`openai.rs:1556`):
   - each branch gets a child context `{id}-{qid}` linked to the parent, so a client disconnect or the first failure cancels all branches;
   - a request deadline cancels all branches and returns 504;
   - a `max_branches` semaphore, separate from request slots, stops a wide fan-out from starving other traffic, and returns 529 with `Retry-After` when full.

   If the pinned worker goes away mid-request, the request fails with 503 instead of rescoring on a cold worker.

6. Handle more than 128 labels. vLLM caps `logprob_token_ids` at 128 (`MAX_LOGPROB_TOKEN_IDS`). The handler splits the labels into chunks of at most 128 with the same prompt and joins the raw logprobs before one softmax.

7. Score (SGLang). A softmax over the raw label logprobs, which gives the same result as SGLang's softmax over the label logits at temperature 1. `noul` is p(yes). `choice` is the most likely option, with ties going to the first option in request order. `score` is the sum of i times p_i. Confidence is computed as described above. Each answer also has `type` and `x_label_mass`, the sum of exp(raw logprob) over the labels, which shows how much of the model's probability landed on the offered labels. A non-finite value fails the request with 500. `model` is the served model name. `usage.input_tokens` is the sum of prompt tokens over the questions, counting each question once, and `usage.output_tokens` is 0.

8. Later (v1.1): permutation debiasing for choice questions, averaging K cyclic shifts of the options with a geometric mean as AnyJev does. It is cheap once the prefix is cached. It stays off by default because it changes the answers compared with SGLang.

### Backend support

| Backend | Status |
|---|---|
| vLLM | Works today. `logprob_token_ids` is allowlisted (`validate.rs:116`), forwarded (`preprocessor.rs:1877`) and applied in the worker (`vllm/handlers.py:855`, which clears `logprobs` because vLLM raises unless `logprobs == len(logprob_token_ids)`). We still need a test showing the IDs come back as raw logprobs, so that `x_label_mass` is exact. The limit is 128 IDs per request (step 6). With speculative decoding, restricted logprobs can crash the rejection sampler ([vLLM issue 42592](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42592), fix pending in [vLLM PR 44727](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44727)), and vLLM's Rust scoring route rejects such engines ([vLLM PR 46427](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46427)). The route should reject those workers too until the fix lands. A faster path for scoring a fixed set of tokens is proposed in [vLLM issue 56767](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56767) and [vLLM PR 56782](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56782). |
| SGLang | Missing. `build_sglang_logprob_kwargs` (`common/backend/logprobs.py:268`) only maps `logprobs` and `prompt_logprobs`. It needs to map `logprob_token_ids` to `return_logprob=True, token_ids_logprob=[...]` and parse `meta_info.output_token_ids_logprobs`. The `DYN_SGL_ALLOW_TOP_LOGPROBS` gate isn't needed since this skips the costly top-k detokenization. SGLang's own route is validated with NEXTN speculative decoding, but it scores through `/v1/score` rather than generation, so PR 1 tests the generation path with speculative decoding on. |
| TRT-LLM | Only top-k logprobs (`handler_base.py:1106`), so labels outside the top k would be missing. Either leave it unsupported or offer best effort with a warning. |

### Reference implementation: SGLang

[SGLang PR 41208](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41208), merged on 2026-09-25, serves the protocol inside one SGLang server. It goes through the `/v1/score` path (`score_prompts` with `apply_softmax=True`), with one prefill per question and no generated text. This DEP matches it on every point the protocol leaves open:

| Topic | SGLang's route | This DEP |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt | One user message: state, blank line, question block, reasoning off (prompt format version 1) | Same (step 2) |
| Labels | `yes`/`no`, `A` to `Z`, `0` to `9`, two-letter labels above 26 options when the template allows | Same (step 3) |
| Limits | 1 to 255 options, 1 to 10 levels | Same, plus request limits |
| Errors | 422 detail list without `input`, 400 when the model or template can't serve the request, 500 for non-finite scores | Same |
| Confidence | Official adapter formulas | Same |
| Response | `type` and `x_label_mass` per answer, served model name, `output_tokens` 0, unrounded values | Same |
| Scale-out | One engine, radix cache shares the prefix | First question places the prefix, the rest are pinned to that worker; several backends |

What the PR and its docs (`docs/docs/supported-models/decision_models.mdx`) report:

- The official Python and JS SDKs work with only the base URL changed. The unofficial `jevcompat` checker passes all 32 of its MUST checks.
- Tested on one H200 in BF16 with Qwen3.8-27B (with and without NEXTN speculative decoding) and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. A request with 62 questions over a 31K-token state takes about 9.5 s, and 64 concurrent requests all return 200. Answers are bitwise equal to SGLang's `/v1/decisions` route on the same prompts.
- Known caveats. On hybrid-attention models (Qwen3.5), probabilities can move by up to 0.07 and label mass by about 0.14 between cold and cached requests or with different batch compositions. The chosen option stayed the same in their tests, and `--disable-radix-cache` makes repeated runs identical. The SDKs also time out after 10 s and retry, so long requests need a higher client timeout.

The same cold versus cached drift can happen in Dynamo, since the first question runs cold and the others hit its cache. Parity tests should use dense models, or allow for SGLang's documented drift.

## Alternatives considered

1. Side-car wrappers only, like openjev-sglang. No changes to engines or Dynamo, but also no routing, no prefix reuse across replicas, no multi-model dispatch and no lifecycle management. This is what exists today, and we reject it as the only option.
2. The frontend extension hook. It only supports GET routes and can't reach engines (see `frontend_extension.rs`).
3. An adapter in an API gateway above Dynamo. This works, but every deployment has to set it up and Dynamo knows nothing about the route. It can live alongside native support but doesn't replace it.
4. Rely on each engine's own route (SGLang's now, vLLM's if it adds one). This works per engine but gives no routing across replicas and no common behavior across backends. Since this DEP matches SGLang, clients can still switch between the two and get the same answers.

## Open questions

SGLang's route already answers the error format, score confidence, `usage`, labels and `x_label_mass`. These are still open:

| Question | Proposal |
|---|---|
| Model naming (`jev-latest` alias?) | When exactly one System One capable model is served, accept any `model` value and return the served name, as SGLang does, so existing Jev clients work unchanged. With several models, require the served name. Aliases belong in a layer above Dynamo. |
| Rounding | Return unrounded values like SGLang. TypeSafe's examples show 2 decimals, and clients that compare strings can round. |
| Prompt format changes | Pin to SGLang's prompt format version 1 and only change it together with SGLang. Document the version on the docs page. |
| Per-request cache salt | Off by default so identical states reuse the prefix across requests. Offer it as an option for tenant isolation, knowing that salting every request turns that reuse off. Dynamo already forwards `cache_salt`. |
| `GET /v1/models` format | Leave Dynamo's OpenAI list as is. The TypeSafe catalog format stays provider-specific. |
| Choice debiasing by default | Single pass in v1, like SGLang. K cyclic shifts behind a flag in v1.1. |

## Implementation plan

1. SGLang backend: pass `logprob_token_ids` through as `token_ids_logprob` and parse the response, with tests, including one with speculative decoding on. This is useful even without System One.
2. Protocol and scoring in Rust (`lib/llm/src/protocols/systemone/`): types, prompt builder, label tokenization, softmax scoring. Unit tests use TypeSafe's documented examples (the score example must give 0.92) and prompt, label and answer vectors generated from SGLang's route for the same inputs.
3. Handler, flag, route, metrics and docs, tested on the vLLM backend. This covers rendering once, token-ID branches, placement and pinning, chunking above 128 labels, the deadline, reasoning checks, and a per-request prefix cache hit ratio (`cached_tokens` / `prompt_tokens`) so prefix reuse can be monitored. Acceptance is measured on JevBench's 231 items, with the same dense model and chat template served by Dynamo and by SGLang's route:
   - identical prompt tokens and label IDs;
   - with the SGLang backend from PR 1, the same chosen option and probabilities within 0.01;
   - with the vLLM backend, the same chosen option on at least 99% of items and a JevBench score within run-to-run noise, since the two engines' kernels differ numerically;
   - the official SDKs work with only the base URL changed, and `jevcompat` passes its MUST checks.
4. Optional: permutation debiasing and calibration knobs (prior, temperature), off by default.

PRs follow the contribution guide (DCO sign-off, Apache-2.0 SPDX headers), and recipes follow `recipes/CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## Future work

Some System One models are not chat models. They use an encoder with small trained heads and answer from embeddings rather than label logprobs, which is less accurate but much faster. Serving them needs a different engine path (an embedding worker plus a component running the heads), so they are out of scope here and could be covered by a separate DEP. Nothing in this DEP blocks that. The handler already resolves `model` to a served model, so a later DEP can register those models and forward their requests while reusing the wire protocol, validation, error formats and test vectors defined here.

## References

- TypeSafe API: https://docs.typesafe.ai/api
- TypeSafe official adapter (confidence formulas): https://github.com/typesafe-ai/system-one-adapter-python
- SGLang `/v1/systemone` PR: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41208 (docs: `docs/docs/supported-models/decision_models.mdx`)
- SGLang `/v1/decisions` PR, closed and merged into the one above: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40992
- SGLang candidate scoring PR: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40826
- vLLM DiffusionGemma structured reads PR (example `/v1/systemone` proxy): https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57250
- vLLM Laya PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58429
- JevBench: https://github.com/fstandhartinger/jevbench
- openjev-sglang: https://github.com/ekzhang/openjev-sglang
- AnyJev: https://github.com/nokia-applied-research/AnyJev
- Standalone servers: https://github.com/razorback16/openjev, https://github.com/yijunyu/jev-rs, https://github.com/TheoLeeCJ/SemIf-OpenJev

title: [BUG]: Worker crash-loop on large models — canary health-check 3s timeout kills fully-loaded workers (v1.5.0)
body:
# [BUG]: Worker crash-loop on large models — canary health-check 3s timeout kills fully-loaded workers (v1.5.0)

## Describe the Bug

Since v1.5.0, the operator enables canary health checks on every worker (`DYN_HEALTH_CHECK_ENABLED=true` for runtime ≥ 1.5.0, gated by the `CanaryHealthChecks` runtime feature). The runtime then requires a canary generate request to complete within **3 seconds** (`DEFAULT_HEALTH_CHECK_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECS = 3`, `lib/runtime/src/config.rs:31`) before the `/live` endpoint returns 200.

For large models (27B+ parameters, fp8 quantization, long context windows), the first generate after engine startup takes far longer than 3 seconds — CUDA graphs are cold, KV cache was just allocated, and no warmup batches have run. The canary times out, the endpoint stays `NotReady`, `/live` returns 503, and the **liveness probe (5s period × 3 failures = 15s budget) kills the fully-loaded worker**. The container restarts, reloads the model from scratch (10-15 minutes), the canary fails again, and the process repeats — an infinite crash loop.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a DGD with a large model (e.g. 27B fp8, 262k context) on vLLM as the runtime, using a v1.5.0+ operator and runtime image
2. The model loads (weights download, CUDA graph capture) — this takes several minutes
3. The first canary health check fires (`canary_wait_time_secs=10` after "no activity detected")
4. The first generate on the cold engine exceeds the 3-second timeout
5. `/live` stays at 503; once the startup probe eventually passes and liveness takes over, the worker is killed within 15 seconds
6. Container restarts → model reloads → canary fails again → **crash loop**

Representative log sequence from a crashing worker:

```
# runtime starts
dynamo runtime configuration: ... starting_health_status=NotReady,
  health_check_enabled=true, canary_wait_time_secs=10, health_check_request_timeout_secs=3

# engine finishes loading (minutes later)
(EngineCore pid=456) Capturing CUDA graphs: 100%|██████████| 11/11 [00:00<00:00]

# canary fires and times out
WARN dynamo_runtime::health_check: Health check timeout for generate

# liveness kills the fully loaded worker
Container main failed liveness probe, will be restarted

# graceful shutdown of a fully-loaded engine
[shutdown] MPClient: stopping engine manager
[shutdown] Process manager: force killing remaining process EngineCore pid 457
```

## Expected Behavior

The canary health check should not kill workers that have successfully loaded their model. Options:

1. **Raise the default timeout** — `DEFAULT_HEALTH_CHECK_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECS` from 3s to 30-60s (a first generate on a cold large model can take 10-60+ seconds)
2. **Let the operator respect a user-set timeout** — the operator force-appends `DYN_HEALTH_CHECK_ENABLED=true` (unconditional env append, so any user-set value for that key is overridden), but it does not set `DYN_HEALTH_CHECK_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`. Users can work around via that env var — but only if they know it exists after already crashlooping
3. **Delay the canary until the engine signals readiness** — rather than firing a synthetic generate against a cold engine, wait for the engine to report that it has completed warmup / is ready to serve
4. **Make the liveness probe not treat a canary timeout as process-dead** — the worker is alive and loaded; only its health payload is "not ready." Liveness (process alive) and readiness (canary passed) should be distinct

## Actual Behavior

- Workers running large models crash-loop: they load the model, the canary generate exceeds 3s, liveness kills them, they reload, repeat indefinitely
- Workers running small models (where the first generate fits in 3s) work fine — making this model-size-dependent and hard to reproduce on small test models
- The startup probe has a generous 2-hour budget (720 × 10s) that correctly accounts for slow model loading, but the canary's 3s timeout and the liveness probe's 15s budget contradict it

## Environment

- ai-dynamo v1.5.0 (upstream release, no local patches touching health checks, operator, or probes)
- Kubernetes, DGD with vLLM backend
- Model: 27B parameters, fp8 quantization, 262144-token context
- The operator's rendered probes for the worker:
  - Startup: `/live`, period 10s, timeout 5s, failureThreshold 720 (2h)
  - Liveness: `/live`, period 5s, timeout 4s, failureThreshold 3 (15s)
- Runtime config as logged by the worker:
  ```
  starting_health_status=NotReady, health_check_enabled=true,
  canary_wait_time_secs=10, health_check_request_timeout_secs=3
  ```

## Additional Context

**Relevant source locations (v1.5.0):**

| Location | What it does |
|---|---|
| `deploy/operator/internal/features/runtime/gates.go:15-18` | `CanaryHealthChecks` gate, `MinRuntimeVersion: 1.5.0` |
| `deploy/operator/internal/dynamo/component_worker.go:51-61` | Operator renders liveness probe (5s × 3 = 15s) |
| `deploy/operator/internal/dynamo/component_worker.go:78-88` | Operator renders startup probe (10s × 720 = 2h) |
| `deploy/operator/internal/dynamo/component_worker.go:90-101` | Operator unconditionally appends `DYN_HEALTH_CHECK_ENABLED=true` |
| `lib/runtime/src/config.rs:29-31` | `DEFAULT_CANARY_WAIT_TIME_SECS = 10`, `DEFAULT_HEALTH_CHECK_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECS = 3` |
| `lib/runtime/src/health_check.rs:195` | "Health check task started" + canary generate loop |
| `lib/runtime/src/health_check.rs:285` | "Health check timeout for generate" — the WARN that precedes the kill |

**Why this matters for large-model users**: NVIDIA's own v1.5.0 recipes include Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.3-Flash on B200/GB200 — all large models that would exceed a 3s cold-start canary. The 3s default effectively makes v1.5.0 canary health checks incompatible with the models the platform is designed to serve.

**The interplay diagram:**

```
[Model loads: 5-15 min]
  /live = 503 (endpoint NotReady, canary hasn't fired yet)
  Startup probe: failing but 2h budget → holds ✅

[Engine ready, canary fires at +10s]
  First generate on cold engine → takes 10-60s
  Times out at 3s ❌ → /live still 503
  Startup probe: still within 2h budget → holds ✅

[Eventually /live goes 200 briefly → startup probe PASSES]
  Liveness probe takes over (15s budget)
  Next canary also takes >3s → /live flips to 503
  Liveness kills the fully loaded worker in 15s ❌

[Container restarts → model reloads → cycle repeats]
  → INFINITE CRASH LOOP
```

**Workaround** (for anyone hitting this now): set `DYN_HEALTH_CHECK_REQUEST_TIMEOUT=60` (or higher) in the worker pod's env. The operator does not set this variable, so the user's value takes effect. This gives the canary enough budget to complete on a cold large-model engine.

title: [BUG]: thinking budget never applies to plain chat with --dyn-chat-processor dynamo
body:
### Describe the Bug

With the default Rust preprocessor (`--dyn-chat-processor dynamo`), SGLang thinking-token budgets never apply to ordinary chat requests.

The Rust preprocessor tells the worker that a request is a reasoning request only when the request is guided, that is when it has a tool choice or a non-text `response_format`. A plain chat request with thinking enabled is not marked, so on the worker SGLang starts its reasoning state machine already in the generation phase. Nothing counts thinking tokens and nothing forces `</think>`, so `--enable-strict-thinking` and `SGLANG_MAX_THINK_TOKENS` have no effect at all for that request.

The result is that on one and the same worker, a plain thinking request reasons until it hits `max_tokens` and returns no answer, while the very same request with a `response_format` added is cut at the configured budget. The only difference is one field in the request body.

The gate is `guided_output_requires_reasoning` in `lib/llm/src/preprocessor.rs` (L1981-1999). The SGLang chat processor has its own copy of the same rule, which is being changed in #14983, but the Rust path is not covered by that PR.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. The worker:
```
python -m dynamo.sglang
--model-path <qwen3-family-reasoning-model>
--dyn-reasoning-parser qwen3 --reasoning-parser qwen3
--enable-strict-thinking
```
with `SGLANG_MAX_THINK_TOKENS=32` in the worker environment.

2. The frontend:
`python -m dynamo.frontend --dyn-chat-processor dynamo`

3. Send a plain thinking request:
```
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
"model": "<model-name>",
"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "How many primes are below 300? Reason step by step."}],
"max_tokens": 2048,
"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "medium"}
}'
```
The response has a very long `reasoning_content`, `content` is empty and `finish_reason` is `length`.

4. Send the same request with one field added:
`"response_format": {"type": "json_object"}`

Now `reasoning_content` stops after 32 tokens and the model produces an answer.

Reasoning length was measured by tokenizing `message.reasoning_content` with the model tokenizer

### Expected Behavior

Under `--dyn-chat-processor dynamo`, a request with thinking enabled should be marked as a reasoning request for the worker, regardless of tool choice or `response_format`.

In step 3 the reasoning should stop at 32 tokens and the model should go on to answer, the same way it does in step 4.

### Actual Behavior

Step 3 is not bounded at all: the request runs to `max_tokens` inside `<think>` and returns `finish_reason: "length"` with empty `content`. Step 4, on the same worker, is cut at exactly 32.

Same worker, 3 runs each:

| request | reasoning tokens | budget applied |
|---|---|---|
| plain thinking chat | 8192 / 7195 / 5884 | no |
| same + `response_format: {"type": "json_schema", ...}` | 32 / 32 / 32 | yes |
| same + `tool_choice: "required"` | 32 / 32 / 32 | yes |

### Environment

- ai-dynamo 1.5.0, SGLang `0.5.20.dev1136+gc79510cc2`, Python 3.12, Linux x86_64, H200, CUDA 12.x

Both the engine-side `--reasoning-parser` and dynamo's `--dyn-reasoning-parser` are set, as Parser Configuration requires for thinking budgets under `--dyn-chat-processor dynamo`. The engine clearly sees its parser: guided requests on this worker are cut at exactly 32 tokens, which is only possible with an active `ReasonerGrammarBackend`.

### Additional Context

Switching to `--dyn-chat-processor sglang` alone does not help: `sglang_prepost.py` has its own copy of the same rule. With a runtime patch making that helper return the resolved per-request thinking decision (the change proposed in #14983), the same worker gives:

| request | reasoning tokens | result |
|---|---|---|
| plain thinking chat | 32 / 32 / 32 | forced `</think>`, then a normal answer |
| `response_format: json_schema` | 32 / 32 / 32 | schema-valid content, `finish_reason: "stop"` |
| `tool_choice: "required"` | 32 / 32 / 32 | one tool call, `finish_reason: "tool_calls"` |

So the engine side works; only the per-request reasoning declaration is missing.

Impact on #15120: its backend part reads `request["stop_conditions"]["max_thinking_tokens"]`, which the Rust preprocessor also populates (root-level `thinking_token_budget` from #12624, or `nvext.max_thinking_tokens`). Once that lands, the Rust path would carry the budget to the worker but fail its `require_reasoning` precondition for plain chat, so the result would be a validation error rather than a budget.

Related: #14983 (same gate on the SGLang chat processor, also raised there), #15120 (thinking token budgets)

### Screenshots

_No response_

title: [FEATURE]: Shared-cache tier for the vLLM MooncakeStoreConnector (--shared-cache-type mooncake-store)
body:
### Feature request

Add a shared-cache tier implementation for the vLLM `MooncakeStoreConnector`, e.g. `--shared-cache-type mooncake-store` (a `VllmMooncakeStore` next to `HicacheSharedKvCache`), so the KV router can see blocks that live only in the shared Mooncake store when the engine is vLLM.

Today `--shared-cache-type hicache` (`lib/llm/src/kv_router/shared_cache.rs`) consumes the Mooncake master's KV-event stream (`ENABLE_KV_EVENTS`, ZMQ PUB of `stored` / `removed` per object) but derives keys with SGLang's HiCache scheme (`{sha256 page hash}_{rank}_k/v` from the `sglang_hicache_mooncake` model card). With a vLLM worker it is inert: the vLLM connector's object keys look like

```
{cache_prefix}@{model}{namespace}@tp_rank:R@pcp0@dcp{D}@pp_rank:0@group:{G}@{chunk_hash_hex}
```

with one Mooncake `group_id` per chunk (`vllm-mooncake-store:{cache_prefix}@{model}{namespace}@{chunk_hash_hex}`) shared by the per-rank / per-KV-group objects, so nothing the hicache client computes ever matches.

### Describe the problem you're encountering

Setup: vLLM main (post vllm#55531) with `MooncakeStoreConnector` as the L3 in a `MultiConnector`, PD disaggregated on GB300 (TP4 / DCP4, hybrid MLA + linear-attention model with two prefix-cacheable KV cache groups), Dynamo frontend at `202478991b`, Mooncake `0.3.13+gb46235d` built from source with `-DENABLE_KV_EVENTS=ON`.

The router indexes only the workers' GPU-tier KV events. The connector's own store events arrive with `medium="cpu"` (lowercase) and are dropped by `StorageTier::from_kv_medium`, which is arguably correct since they describe a rack-shared pool, not the publishing worker's host tier. The result is that a prefix that is fully present in the shared store is scored as cold, so worker selection ignores L3 locality and, for anyone using booked prefill tokens for admission, the request is booked as a full cold prefill.

Points that shaped the design we ended up with, in case they help whoever picks this up:

- vLLM's chunk hash is sha256 over a pickled `(parent_hash, tokens, extra_keys)` chained from a process-seeded `NONE_HASH`, so the router cannot recompute the keys from tokens the way the hicache client does. But the workers' GPU `stored` events already carry the exact chain: `KvCacheStoredBlockData { block_hash (external, u64 = low 64 bits of the chunk hash), tokens_hash }` plus `parent_hash`. Learning a `(parent_external, tokens_hash) -> external` map from those events, tapped in `Indexer::try_apply_event` before the radix tree's parent check (so events rejected as `parent_block_not_found` still teach the chain), gives router-granularity keys with zero dependence on vLLM's pickle format.
- Presence can be keyed by the chunk hash parsed from the event's `group_id` (trailing hex after the last `@`) rather than `object_key`, which collapses the `dcp × groups` objects of one chunk into one entry. A `removed` for the group should drop the chunk (the engine needs every rank namespace present, so a partial chunk must read as a miss). A sequence gap or subscriber reconnect should clear presence but keep the learned chain.
- Lookup then walks the chain over the request's per-block `LocalBlockHash`es and returns the prefix run, since the connector can only extend a prefix.
- The chain map needs a bound that fits real stores (the existing `MAX_MOONCAKE_INDEX_ENTRIES` of 1,000,000 is far below a multi-TB store's key count); a two-generation sweep works.
- Useful extra metrics: present entries, chain entries, and blocks that stopped on a missing chain link rather than an absent hash (tells whether learning coverage is the bottleneck).
- Mooncake side: the publisher is a compile-time option that upstream defaults off, and its `dependencies.sh` only installs libzmq on the Debian/Ubuntu branch, so a manylinux (AlmaLinux) wheel build needs `zeromq-devel` added by hand before configure.

### Describe alternatives you've tried

- `--shared-cache-type hicache` against the vLLM connector: inert, as above.
- Admitting the connector's lowercase `cpu` events as a host tier: wrong, it would credit rack-shared blocks as host residency of one worker and double count against the disk weight.
- We implemented the approach above as a patch on our frontend build (new `SharedCacheType::MooncakeStore`, `SharedKvCache::observe_stored` / `check_blocks_by_local_hashes` trait additions, `Arc<dyn SharedKvCache>` shared between the router and the indexer), and it passes the kv-router and dynamo-llm test suites. Happy to share it as a reference for whoever takes this upstream; a native implementation would let us drop the patch.

title: [FEATURE]: ThunderAgent shared-prefix accounting: GPU A/B/C results with explicit headroom
body:
<!-- thunderagent-current-status-20260921:start -->
## Summary and current status — 2026-09-21

**Problem under investigation:** the tested ThunderAgent accounting charges each ACTIVE program's full context separately, even when programs on the same replica share an exact prefix. The measurements examine logical shared-prefix accounting with explicit growth headroom. B is still a benchmark-only oracle that knows the synthetic sharing relationships, not a production implementation driven by cache-residency signals.

**Latest complete comparison:** 35 rows with 16 existing + 16 new programs and equal KV-pool capacity in all configurations. In the exact-sharing condition, original A reached 28 sampled ACTIVE programs (16 existing + 12 new); B reached 32. Across three paired blocks, B64 increased batch throughput by **54.66%**, while existing-program P50/P95 increased by **4.50%/4.73%**. The entire measured batch completed about **35.34% sooner**. The slowdown concerns existing programs in this measured phase, not a slowdown of the entire batch or full agent lifetime. [Full experiment data](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/15105#issuecomment-5753953622).

**Observed limitation:** lowering B's backend execution cap to 28/30 increased existing-program P95 by **33.15%/32.91%** relative to A; qualification traces showed existing requests waiting at those limits. A cap of 32 produced a **5.19%** increase. B64 met this matrix's diagnostic gates; B28/B30/B32 failed the existing-P95 gate. All zero-sharing gates passed. The earlier mixed experiment's slightly-over-5% verdict and the preliminary capacity-mismatch failure remain preserved.

**Timing clarification:** a post-hoc client timing split found nearly unchanged mean time to first output (**2.637 → 2.632 s**) and longer time after first output (**8.803 → 9.342 s**). This is consistent with contention during concurrent generation. The exact slowdown onset and causal contribution of arrival timing are not established. These are request-clock arithmetic means, not cohort P95 or engine-only compute measurements. [Timing analysis and definitions](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/15105#issuecomment-5766571823).

**Evidence boundary:** the fixed-KV matrix completed 35/35 rows with zero observed preemption increments and complete data audits. Results are scoped to one worker/one physical GPU, synthetic workloads and three paired blocks per condition; actual generated histories differ in some pairs. No production readiness, general safe headroom, cluster-wide gain or confirmed remedy is claimed. The original A/B/C study below and later comments cover different workloads; their results are not pooled.

<!-- thunderagent-current-status-20260921:end -->

---

### Feature request

Investigate shared-prefix-aware program accounting with explicit growth headroom in ThunderAgent. I ran a single-replica GPU experiment comparing unchanged accounting, an idealized deduplication prototype, and threshold-only tuning.

**At 90% initial sharing, the prototype improved program completion throughput by 30.2% versus unchanged accounting (95% paired bootstrap interval: 23.6–37.3%), and reduced program P95 by 23.2%, but increased P50 by 16.9%.** This is a scoped throughput/tail improvement with a median-latency tradeoff, not a general latency win or a production-ready implementation.

The motivation was a Slack discussion in which the repeated accounting was described as implicit buffer/headroom and investigating deduplication was encouraged. That discussion was encouragement to investigate, not approval of this implementation or its performance claims.

### Describe the problem you're encountering

In the tested [scheduler source](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/4df3f3af83dd1e6ffd36d7c0a152b4efdd85f30f/components/src/dynamo/thunderagent_router/router.py#L455), `_replica_usage_locked()` adds each ACTIVE program's token total plus a per-program buffer. An exact prefix shared by multiple programs is therefore charged repeatedly, even when the backend reuses it. [Capacity discovery](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/4df3f3af83dd1e6ffd36d7c0a152b4efdd85f30f/components/src/dynamo/thunderagent_router/capacity.py) and the backend's physical occupancy signals have different semantics; this report does not infer waste merely from apparently unused GPU memory.

A preceding unchanged-scheduler pilot covered 0/50/90% sharing and 2/4/8/16/32 programs: no pauses at the tested 2–16 levels, but the 32-program level initially admitted 28 at every sharing level. Exact token-prefix checks and backend cache hits confirmed reuse. This established the accounting/concurrency question; it did not establish a deduplication speedup. The A/B/C results below are the subsequent controlled comparison, not speedups computed across different sharing workloads.

### Describe alternatives you've tried

| Arm | Accounting and settings |
|---|---|
| A | Original installed scheduler/accounting: 100-token per-program buffer; pause threshold/target/resume hysteresis = 0.95/0.80/0.10. |
| B | Benchmark-only **known-synthetic-prefix oracle**: charge complete shared prefix blocks once per active family, rounded private token slots per program, and a separate 256-token growth reserve per ACTIVE program. Uses the original pause thresholds. |
| C | Original accounting and 100-token buffer, with existing pause threshold/target/resume hysteresis tuned to 0.97/0.90/0.05. |

B and C each received three calibration candidates, with the same zero/high-sharing calibration workload and eligibility rule. Parameters were then frozen before held-out validation. All candidates, including unfavorable results, are retained below. C is the selected candidate from this bounded search, not a globally optimal threshold configuration; default A was itself faster than selected C on primary validation, so **B/A is the main comparison**.

B's accounting is rebuilt from ACTIVE membership on admission, pause, resume and completion/cancellation. Removing one program retains a shared-family charge while another ACTIVE program still uses it. A logical accounting decrease is not a claim of immediate backend memory release. The prototype changes accounting/admission checks in a local benchmark subclass, without editing installed Dynamo files, KV layout, or cross-replica placement. It assumes ACTING weight 1 and one compatible replica; no semantic similarity, adapters, or production cache index.

### Held-out GPU results

| Initial sharing | Paired blocks | B/A throughput [95% CI] | B/C throughput [95% CI] | B/A P50 [95% CI] | B/A P95 [95% CI] |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 90% (primary) | 12 | 1.302 [1.236, 1.373] | 1.401 [1.267, 1.548] | 1.169 [1.114, 1.232] | 0.768 [0.728, 0.809] |
| 50% (secondary) | 3 | 1.242 [1.149, 1.306] | 1.294 [1.214, 1.337] | 1.119 [1.101, 1.139] | 0.805 [0.766, 0.870] |
| 0% (regression control) | 3 | 1.002 [0.993, 1.019] | 1.013 [1.003, 1.023] | 0.992 [0.980, 1.000] | 0.998 [0.981, 1.007] |

Ratios are geometric means of paired batch ratios. Throughput ratios above 1 are better; P50/P95 ratios above 1 are worse. Intervals use 10,000 bootstrap resamples of **whole paired batches**, seed 20260919; programs/tokens are not treated as independent repetitions. The three-block secondary checks have limited precision.

Absolute arithmetic means for the 12 primary blocks (these are a different aggregation from the paired geometric ratios):

| 90% initial sharing | Batch completion, s | Completed programs/s | Program P50, s | Program P95, s | Sampled peak ACTIVE programs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 56.695 | 0.566 | 37.165 | 56.692 | 28 |
| B | 43.608 | 0.738 | **43.560** | 43.606 | 32 |
| C | 61.368 | 0.530 | 41.729 | 61.365 | 28 |

Program completion time runs from scheduled arrival through the third inference response, including scheduler waiting and simulated tool waits. Batch time runs from the batch arrival origin to the last completed program; throughput is completed programs divided by that time. Per-batch P50/P95 use nearest-rank percentiles of 32 program times; they are not a long-running production latency distribution.

**Observed:**

- All **54/54 held-out validation rows** completed and passed input, lifecycle, route, capacity and accounting audits: 18 paired blocks, each containing A/B/C. Across qualification, overhead checks, calibration and validation, 78 valid rows completed 2,238 programs / 6,714 inference calls. One additional pre-measurement infrastructure failure is retained.
- At 50/90% sharing, B admitted all 32 programs without budget pauses; A/C initially admitted 28 and recorded 32 pause events per batch. At zero sharing, all arms recorded 32 pause events. Pause counts explain behavior; they are not the success metric.
- Backend preemption counter increments were zero in every validation row; backend generation-counter deltas matched actual streamed output tokens. No validation request failures were observed. The backend log scan found no ERROR/traceback/OOM records; authoritative backend failure/OOM counters remain unavailable, and this is not a general safety guarantee.
- At 90% sharing, each arm had the same per-batch request-usage-derived `sum(prompt_tokens - cached_tokens)` = **132,608**; at 50%, **315,392**. Thus the measured gain did not require reducing this observable prompt-work proxy. At zero sharing, B's mean proxy was approximately 0.9% higher than A's. This proxy is not total engine recomputation.
- The zero-sharing B/A P95 interval was 0.981–1.007, within the predeclared 1.05 margin for these three held-out blocks. This does not establish regression freedom for arbitrary zero-sharing workloads.

**Possible explanation:** earlier admission gives the last-finishing programs less scheduler waiting, improving makespan and P95, while increased concurrency makes some earlier-finishing programs contend longer and worsens P50. The observations support a scheduling opportunity, not faster individual GPU token computation.

### Reproduction scope and controls

| Item | Fixed configuration |
|---|---|
| Hardware | One NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, 97,887 MiB; driver 590.44.01; one inference worker, TP=1/DP=1. |
| Software | Python 3.12.13; ai-dynamo and ai-dynamo-runtime 1.5.0.dev20260917; vLLM 0.29.0; Torch 2.13.0+cu130; Transformers 5.17.0. |
| Source provenance | Installed `router.py`, `capacity.py`, `program_state.py`, `__main__.py`, `args.py` byte-match commit `4df3f3af83dd1e6ffd36d7c0a152b4efdd85f30f`. Native wheel build commit was not independently established; native artifacts were separately hashed. This is not a claim that current main has identical behavior. |
| Model | Qwen/Qwen3-8B, revision `b968826d9c46dd6066d109eabc6255188de91218`. |
| Backend | BF16; prefix caching; 64-token blocks; eager mode; max model length 18,432; max sequences 64; max batched tokens 8,192; GPU memory utilization 0.85. GPU-only, no native offload. |
| Capacity | Same discovered budget in all measured arms: 468,736 token slots / 7,324 blocks. |
| Programs | 32 programs in **four independent prefix families of eight**; 16,384 initial input tokens, 256 actual generated tokens per turn, three turns; append actual generated IDs plus 256 tool-result tokens between turns. |
| Sharing | Exact token-ID prefixes of 0 / 8,192 / 14,745 tokens per family. B only deduplicates complete blocks: 0 / 8,192 / 14,720 tokens. |
| Primary validation | 90% initial sharing, 2 s tool wait, burst; 12 fresh seeds 600–611; all six A/B/C execution orders twice. |
| Secondary validation | 0/50% sharing, 1 s tool wait, 5 ms arrival jitter; three fresh seeds per sharing level (700–702 / 710–712), cyclic arm orders. |
| Scheduler/measurement | Original 5 s tick; arrival phases 0.25/1.75/3.25 s after a completed tick, matched across each block and checked within 100 ms. 250 ms sampling. |

Actual shared-prefix ratios were reconstructed from token IDs at every turn, rather than assumed constant:

| Initial group | Turn 1 | Turn 2 | Turn 3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0% | 0.000% | 0.000% | 0.000% |
| 50% | 50.000% | 48.485% | 47.059% |
| 90% | 89.996% | 87.269% | 84.702% |

Every row used a fresh router with the same backend and the same two-request warmup sequence (512 input / 16 output tokens per request), then an explicit backend cache reset and empty-state checks. Warmup and fixture construction were excluded from timing. All arms used the same prefix validation and measurement wrapper; no client concurrency semaphore. This used Dynamo's native token endpoint, so there was no chat-template-added common prefix or HTTP frontend in the measurement.

Before calibration, three N=8, 50%-sharing sampler-on/off pairs gave a batch-time ratio geometric mean of **0.9996**, below the predeclared 5% overhead gate. This isolates incremental sampler cost, not every logging cost. Measured rows had a 240 s deadline. Failures stopped the campaign; unfavorable valid samples were not rerun or replaced, and validation sample counts were not extended after seeing results.

<details>
<summary>All calibration candidates and selection rule</summary>

B reserves: 256 / 512 / 1,024 tokens per ACTIVE program. C threshold/target/hysteresis triples: 0.97/0.90/0.05, 0.99/0.95/0.02, 1.00/1.00/0.00. Each candidate used the same seed 520 at 0% and 90% sharing, with A references. Eligibility required zero-sharing batch time and P95 no more than 5% above A, zero observed preemption increments, complete output and fresh generation counters. Among eligible candidates, select fastest high-sharing throughput, then freeze.

| Candidate | Zero-share batch, s | High-share batch, s | Eligibility |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| A reference | 105.786 | 49.279 | Reference |
| B, reserve 256 | 109.256 | 40.079 | Eligible; selected |
| B, reserve 512 | 120.979 | 39.837 | Rejected: zero-share regression |
| B, reserve 1,024 | 112.539 | 39.807 | Rejected: zero-share regression |
| C, 0.97/0.90/0.05 | 107.055 | 52.200 | Eligible; selected |
| C, 0.99/0.95/0.02 | 106.144 | 68.159 | Eligible, slower |
| C, 1.00/1.00/0.00 | 115.095 | 62.437 | Rejected: zero-share regression |

The slightly faster high-sharing B candidates were not chosen by overlooking zero-sharing regressions.

</details>

### Limitations and next step

1. **B knows the synthetic sharing relationships in advance**, validates actual request prefixes against them, and does not infer backend residency. A production implementation needs trustworthy existing block identities/shared references and conservative behavior for unknown or stale information. Complete physical shared-reference/residency measurements and total engine recomputation remain **TBD**.
2. Backend cache-hit token counts are not deductible physical bytes. The tested vLLM usage gauge counts non-free blocks and excludes reclaimable cached blocks; its denominator excludes the null block. It cannot simply be subtracted from ThunderAgent's logical retention estimate to obtain a physical estimation error. GPU capacity, any offload capacity and growth reserve must remain distinct.
3. **Every one of the 36 B/C validation batches had at least one generated sequence different from paired A**, despite identical initial token IDs and matched output lengths. Actual generated histories were retained and fed into later turns. The cause has not been isolated, and semantic task equivalence/quality was not evaluated.
4. The P50 regression is material. These are synthetic finite batches on one GPU/model/backend in eager mode, not a claim about real tools, sustained arrivals, CUDA graph configurations, offload, adapters or clusters. C's search and secondary sample sizes are small.

The result supports continuing a narrowly scoped accounting investigation. A useful next step would be to agree on an existing source of same-replica, cache-compatible block identity/reference information, then validate a conservative implementation with the same A/B/C controls, explicit growth reserve, lifecycle accounting invariants and throughput/P50/P95/preemption gates. This report does not request merging the oracle prototype. The input/metric semantics also relate to [admission-control follow-ups #14823](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/14823).

### Data and audit trail

The appendix includes **all 79 A/B/C campaign attempts** as a compact CSV, preserving original numeric precision and `TBD` values. Only the local raw-file-path column is removed. All rows are included, but the headline comparisons use only `stage=validation` and `audit=PASS` with complete A/B/C blocks. A small standalone analysis script is included to reproduce the paired intervals from this CSV.

The full harness, frozen manifests, actual token histories, time series and raw logs are retained locally; **they are not attached to this issue, so this issue alone does not provide a full GPU rerun bundle**. The complete A/B/C archive is approximately 4.4 GB uncompressed / 66.7 MB compressed. Local raw-data reconstruction matched the remote row table, audit, comparisons and report byte-for-byte. These hashes identify retained artifacts; they are not download links:

```text
archive SHA256: 5228236e96f5fdf00d0f5ed8a9614e2b3e66a7743fd4ba9fdab5f4d095210903
original rows.csv SHA256: 45430a8dd54a782d39b685434cfce4656b4f2c0770c82eabc7ae84c35b9ece17
comparisons.json SHA256: 8f208279c8a770547ab2806fbab280a5a625432697c6605af415bf9e8987e373
public compact CSV SHA256: c1c36f3b279b0ff810c470451abfc1fd1a4c3c73e5f4fdb0ad294be768fc97fb
```

One early overhead row failed before measured work because transient discovery selected a stopped router. It and the preceding valid overhead row remain in the appendix. Before calibration, the harness was fixed to verify the intended router identity and select it using existing `Client.direct`, identically for all arms; this did not select backend placement. The entire overhead stage was repeated under separate `v2` IDs with unchanged settings.
