title: Make LPU eviction cleanup durable after trigger Pod deletion
body:
## Summary

Make node-local LPU eviction cleanup durable when the disrupted trigger Pod is deleted before the eviction reconciler processes it.

## Rationale

The current eviction flow enqueues a deleting trigger Pod. If Kubernetes deletes that Pod before reconciliation, `Reconcile` treats the missing Pod as completed. Matching sibling Pods can remain active. This can leave the LPU workload without coordinated replacement during disruption.

## Affected area

- `deploy/operator/internal/controller/lpx/eviction.go`
- LPU eviction watch, predicate, reconciliation, and sibling cleanup logic

## Required changes

Use a durable owner or cohort trigger that survives trigger-Pod deletion. For example, reconcile through the owning `PodClique` or another durable cohort identity. Do not mark cleanup complete when the trigger Pod is missing until the matching cohort has been processed.

Preserve the existing safety behavior:
- Delete only matching sibling Pods.
- Preserve native replacements.
- Keep ownership, UID, resource-version, template-revision, and runtime-partition validation.

## Acceptance criteria

- A disrupted LPU trigger Pod can disappear before the queued reconciliation runs.
- The controller still identifies and cleans up eligible sibling Pods.
- Native replacements and unrelated Pods remain preserved.
- Tests cover deletion of the trigger Pod before reconciliation.

## Backlinks

- Pull request: https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/15062
- Review comment: https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/15062#discussion_r4049895529
- Requested by: @andrewpaprotsky

title: DEP: Cross-replica PolicyClass fairness contract
body:
## Summary

PolicyClass queue and deficit-round-robin (DRR) state is local to each router. In a two-frontend reproducer, a configured 4:1 `premium:regular` share remained near 4:1 when each replica received demand from both classes, but fell near 1:1 when each class reached a different replica.

This DEP has two phases. Phase 1 documents the current router-local contract so deployments do not infer an aggregate guarantee Dynamo does not provide. Phase 2 pursues an ingress-independent aggregate weighted-share guarantee. This DEP recommends one logical PolicyClass scheduler owner per scheduling domain as the first implementation.

## Current behavior

Each router maintains its own PolicyClass queues, DRR deficits, ring position, and counters. Replica synchronization does not provide a shared PolicyClass queue or DRR budget.

For this discussion, a *scheduling domain* is the contention scope formed by PolicyClasses competing for the same eligible worker capacity. The eligible worker set defines the capacity boundary. The PolicyClasses are the participants.

## Evidence

The reproducer used one shared CPU Mocker worker, identical worker eligibility, equal-cost 512-token prompts, replica synchronization, and a 4:1 `premium:regular` policy.

| Topology and ingress              | Premium booked cost | Regular booked cost | Equivalent requests |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------: | ------------------: | ------------------: |
| One frontend                      |              130560 |               33280 |              255:65 |
| Two frontends, balanced per class |              133120 |               34304 |              260:67 |
| Two frontends, direct skew        |               83456 |               82944 |             163:162 |
| Two frontends, swapped skew       |               82944 |               83456 |             162:163 |

Direct skew sends `premium` only to frontend A and `regular` only to frontend B. Swapped skew reverses the placement. Both skewed cases remain near 1:1.

These are successful-booking scheduling-cost counters from a bounded observation window. Prometheus polling can include bookings beyond the sampler’s 320-booking target. The result establishes topology-dependent behavior in this setup. It does not establish a general fairness bound under balanced ingress.

## Proposed current contract

PolicyClass scheduling state and its weighted scheduling decisions are local to each router. Dynamo makes no ingress-independent aggregate PolicyClass share guarantee across router replicas today.

Aggregate behavior depends on how each class’s scheduling-cost demand and backlog reach those replicas. Balancing total HTTP request counts is not enough to ensure that competing classes reach each local scheduler. Dynamo does not enforce per-class ingress distribution.

## Phase 1: Document Current Semantics

Document this behavior and its deployment assumption. A documentation PR carries the wording and focused validation. The booked scheduling-cost metric remains a separate, reviewable change if router owners find it useful.

Phase 1 does not change scheduling behavior. It makes the present limitation explicit and establishes the contract that Phase 2 replaces.

## Phase 2: Cross-Replica Fairness

Phase 2 aims to provide ingress-independent aggregate PolicyClass fairness for each scheduling domain. Its initial scope is an isolated eligible worker set and every PolicyClass that can book work on it. No PolicyClass outside the domain may book a worker in that set. A participating PolicyClass may not book outside it. Classes with overlapping eligibility sets require a later design.

For continuously backlogged classes in one Phase 2 domain, the configured weighted share must hold in successful-booking scheduling-cost units over an exact fixed window, within a documented DRR deviation bound. The bound must account for the maximum request cost and outstanding reservations.

This DEP recommends one logical scheduler owner per domain as the first implementation. Phase 2 is not ready for implementation approval until the domain eligibility rule and the measurable share bound are specified.

The recommended implementation uses one logical scheduler owner per domain:

1. A forwarding router classifies a request and sends its admission intent to the domain owner.
2. The owner is authoritative for the domain's PolicyClass queues, DRR deficits, ring position, and reservations.
3. The owner selects and books work. The forwarding router sends the selected request to the worker.
4. If the owner is unavailable, admission returns an explicit retriable error rather than falling back to independent local scheduling and weakening the guarantee.

Phase 2 deliberately excludes replicated DRR budgets, automatic owner election, and splitting one scheduling domain across multiple owners. Those are scale and availability extensions. Revisit them after the initial single-owner implementation establishes the fairness contract.

The Phase 2 PR must establish the guarantee with an exact successful-booking scheduling-cost window across the existing one-frontend, balanced, direct-skew, and swapped-skew cases. The test placement and harness mechanics belong in that PR.

## Requested decision

**Do you agree with this phased direction: document the router-local contract and ingress assumption in Phase 1, then specify and pursue ingress-independent aggregate PolicyClass fairness in Phase 2?** I recommend yes.

This decision approves the product direction and sequencing. It does not approve a Phase 2 implementation and only recommends the single-owner design.

## References

* [PolicyClass multi-replica discussion](https://ai-dynamo.slack.com/archives/C0BEFAUFE5V/p1788228544878949)
* PolicyClass prioritization test: #12465
* Shared `SelectionCore` DEP: #14310
* Worker-taint synchronization DEP: #12050
* [Measurement instrumentation](https://github.com/tryambak2019/dynamo/commit/6fb6b7029ea7b5722918fd27a2c09aea61ad99ae)
* [PolicyClass documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/dynamo/latest/knowledge-base/modular-components/router/configuration-and-tuning#policy-class-queues)

title: DEP (light): Explicit roles for compound components
body:
## Summary

Introduce explicit `roles` as the internal structure of compound Dynamo components. A component remains the logical inference, lifecycle, scaling, service, rollout, and status unit; roles expose its distinct Pod-producing parts. The first use case is a multinode engine with `leader` and `worker` roles, allowing role-specific provider configuration without turning those roles into sibling DGD components. Existing manifests without `roles` retain their implicit behavior. Complete multinode role PodTemplates and their component-status projection are tracked by the follow-up DEP [#12696](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/12696).

The 1.5 foundation in [#14419](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14419) deliberately excludes `roles[].replicas` and `roles[].podTemplate`. The additive role-cardinality API in [#14477](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14477) and the deny-by-default shared PodTemplate field in [#14544](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14544) have also merged. Multinode cardinality remains determined by `multinode.nodeCount`; the shared PodTemplate field does not itself enable role-template mode.

## Motivation

Dynamo components are already compound. A multinode engine is one logical component but produces a leader and one or more worker Pods. The Grove path lowers those Pods into multiple PodCliques within one PodCliqueScalingGroup. GMS can add further internal Pod roles. Today most of this structure is implicit.

[#12696](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/12696) needs different leader and worker Pod configuration. Its original API direction kept the component `podTemplate` as the leader and common base, then added a restricted `multinode.worker.podTemplateOverrides` overlay. That solves the immediate case but establishes a multinode-specific patch language.

The provider-native override API exposed the same structural issue. [#13273](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13273) added `multinode.leader.providerOverride` and `multinode.worker.providerOverride`. These fields model internal roles but place them inside a multinode-specific structure.

Leader and worker are not independently meaningful graph nodes. They form one mandatory engine, scale as complete engine instances, and expose one component-level service and readiness result. Grouping graph-level components and structuring the inside of one component are different concerns.

The API should expose the existing compound structure inward while preserving the component as Dynamo's inference-aware semantic boundary.

## Proposal

### Semantic model

A role is a named, type-defined part of one component:

- The component remains the DGD graph node.
- `component.replicas` remains the number of complete component instances.
- The component owns rollout, scaling, Service identity, discovery, lifecycle, aggregate status, and the provider-neutral facts consumed by higher-level controllers.
- A role may produce one or more Pods and may lower to a provider-specific workload unit such as a Grove PodClique.
- A role is not independently deployable, routable, or scalable unless a future component-type contract explicitly says otherwise.
- Provider resource names are not role identity and are not exposed through this API.

Allowed role names, required membership, cardinality, and role-specific configuration are defined by the enclosing component type. Users cannot attach arbitrary roles to a component type that does not define them.

This is inward composition:

```text
component: decode
└── roles
    ├── leader
    └── worker
```

It is distinct from grouping graph-level components:

```text
component group
├── component A
└── component B
```

### 1.5 API foundation

Add a map-keyed role list to `DynamoComponentDeploymentSharedSpec`:

```go
type ComponentRoleSpec struct {
    // Name identifies a role within the enclosing component. The component
    // type defines the allowed and required names.
    Name string `json:"name"`

    // ProviderOverride configures the provider-native workload unit generated
    // for this role. Its availability follows the existing DGD/provider rules.
    ProviderOverride *ProviderOverride `json:"providerOverride,omitempty"`
}

type DynamoComponentDeploymentSharedSpec struct {
    // Existing fields...

    // +optional
    // +listType=map
    // +listMapKey=name
    Roles []ComponentRoleSpec `json:"roles,omitempty"`
}
```

The JSON API is a typed list keyed by semantic `name`, not an unstructured map or a list keyed by generated workload names.

`roles[].replicas` and `roles[].podTemplate` are not part of this first delivery. They are independent additive follow-ups. Keeping them out makes the initial API and its 1.5 backport a structural migration of existing role-scoped provider overrides rather than a change to multinode cardinality or Pod rendering.

### Multinode contract

Multinode is the first closed role schema. `multinode.nodeCount` remains authoritative and means the total number of Pods/nodes in one complete multinode engine instance.

```text
component.replicas  = complete engine instances
multinode.nodeCount = Pods/nodes per engine instance
leader Pods         = 1 per engine instance
worker Pods         = multinode.nodeCount - 1 per engine instance
```

When `roles` is absent, current behavior remains:

```yaml
replicas: 2
multinode:
  nodeCount: 8
podTemplate: ...
```

When `roles` is present, it must contain the complete, closed role set:

```yaml
spec:
  components:
  - name: decode
    type: worker
    replicas: 2
    multinode:
      nodeCount: 8
    roles:
    - name: leader
    - name: worker
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: main
          image: example/engine:latest
```

Both forms create two complete engines, each with one leader and seven workers. An explicit list containing only `leader` or only `worker` is invalid. The operator does not synthesize missing role entries.

### ProviderOverride migration

Move the existing multinode role-level paths:

```text
multinode.leader.providerOverride -> roles[name=leader].providerOverride
multinode.worker.providerOverride -> roles[name=worker].providerOverride
```

`MultinodeSpec` keeps only `nodeCount`:

```go
type MultinodeSpec struct {
    NodeCount int32 `json:"nodeCount"`
}
```

The root and component fields remain unchanged because they address different provider scopes:

```text
spec.providerOverride                 -> graph-level provider resource
components[].providerOverride         -> primary component workload unit
components[].roles[].providerOverride -> workload unit for one internal role
```

For Grove, these currently correspond to a PodCliqueSet, a component PodClique or PodCliqueScalingGroup, and an internal role's PodClique template. This mapping is lowering behavior, not role identity.

A worker-only topology override still declares both roles:

```yaml
roles:
- name: leader
- name: worker
  providerOverride:
    apiVersion: grove.io/v1alpha1
    target: PodCliqueTemplateSpec
    value:
      topologyConstraint:
        topologyName: cluster
        pack:
          required: rack
```

### Compatibility and rollout

The multinode `leader` and `worker` provider-override fields were introduced for the upcoming 1.5 API. The structural correction should land before those paths become a released contract.

Existing manifests without `roles` preserve their rendered workload, rollout identity, and implicit multinode behavior. A deployment may make the fixed `{leader, worker}` structure explicit without changing or rolling the rendered workload when neither role carries provider-specific behavior. The reverse transition is equivalent only when removing roles does not discard role-specific configuration.

The role structure is shared by embedded DGD components and standalone DCD specs. Provider-native overrides retain their DGD/provider-specific exposure restrictions.

### Multinode PodTemplate follow-up — tracked by #12696

The following records design context for [#12696](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/12696). Its implementation and validation are completion criteria for that follow-up, not for this roles DEP. #12696 adds complete role-specific PodTemplates to the established role entries without changing component semantics:

```yaml
roles:
- name: leader
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: main
        image: example/engine-leader:latest
- name: worker
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: main
        image: example/engine-worker:latest
```

Role-template mode is a Planner-runtime-dependent feature. Planner versions through 1.5 discover model, runtime, GPU, and power facts from `components[].podTemplate`, which is intentionally absent in this mode. If a DGD contains any `type: planner` component, every Planner must therefore resolve to Dynamo runtime 1.6.0 or later before any component may use `roles[].podTemplate`.

Admission resolves the Planner component's `runtimeVersionOverride` when it is set; otherwise it derives the version from the Planner image tag. The override is authoritative and does not change the image. This gate applies to Planner components, not to the Leader or Worker runtime images. A DGD without a Planner component and a DGD that stays in global-template mode have no new version restriction.

For example, this is valid even when the engine role images themselves remain on 1.5:

```yaml
spec:
  components:
  - name: planner
    type: planner
    runtimeVersionOverride: 1.6.0
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: main
          image: example/custom-planner-build
  - name: decode
    type: decode
    multinode:
      nodeCount: 2
    roles:
    - name: leader
      podTemplate:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: main
            image: example/engine:1.5.0
    - name: worker
      podTemplate:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: main
            image: example/engine:1.5.0
```

The same DGD is rejected if the Planner resolves to 1.5.x or earlier. A transition from the shared component PodTemplate to role-specific PodTemplates may atomically upgrade the Planner to 1.6 or later in the same update.

The operator, not each consumer, resolves the complete role templates. For multinode, `leader` is the serving role. Both the DCD/LeaderWorkerSet path and the Grove path publish the same component-level projection from the fully rendered serving Pod:

```yaml
status:
  observedGeneration: 7
  components:
    decode:
      servedModelName: Qwen/Qwen3-8B
      runtimeComponentName: custom-decode
      gpuPowerLimitWatts: 300
      gpusPerEngine: 8
      gpusPerReplica: 8
```

`servedModelName` and `runtimeComponentName` are omitted when the rendered command does not declare the corresponding model or endpoint override. `gpuPowerLimitWatts` is omitted when no component-level power limit is configured. `gpusPerEngine` and `gpusPerReplica` keep their existing explicit-zero and unavailable semantics.

Consumers such as the Planner read only current component status (`status.observedGeneration == metadata.generation`). They do not inspect `podTemplate`, select a role, or depend on provider workload names. During a worker rolling update, the status projection continues to describe the old active revision until cutover, together with the existing runtime namespace.

This projection is intentionally narrow. It covers the values whose old `components[].podTemplate` lookup becomes ambiguous once leader and worker can have different complete templates: served model name, endpoint component override, GPU shape, and per-GPU power limit. It does not expose the role structure as a second consumer API.

Complete role-specific PodTemplates do not turn roles into sibling components or independent scale targets.

### Role cardinality follow-up

The 1.5 API does not expose role cardinality. Multinode does not need it because `nodeCount` already defines the fixed leader/worker shape.

[#14477](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14477) added optional `roles[].replicas`. For multinode, admission derives and persists `leader = 1` and `worker = multinode.nodeCount - 1` when omitted, and checks authored values against that same fixed shape. Other component types can define their own role-cardinality contracts; multinode roles are not independently scalable.

### Validation

Admission for the 1.5 foundation covers:

| Configuration | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Multinode, no roles | Valid; current implicit behavior |
| Complete `leader`/`worker` roles | Valid; cardinality still comes from `nodeCount` |
| Update from implicit roles to an equivalent explicit list | Valid; representation-only migration |
| Update from explicit roles to implicit roles without losing role settings | Valid |
| Only leader or only worker | Invalid |
| Unknown or duplicate role | Invalid |
| Roles on a type without a role schema | Invalid |
| Complete roles, provider override only on worker | Valid |
| Role provider override on a standalone DCD | Rejected by the standalone OpenAPI schema |

The following role-template cases belong to the [#12696](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/12696) follow-up and are not completion criteria for this DEP:

| Configuration | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Role PodTemplates with no Planner component | Valid; no Planner consumer is present |
| Role PodTemplates with every Planner resolving to runtime 1.6.0 or later | Valid |
| Role PodTemplates with any Planner resolving below runtime 1.6.0 | Invalid |
| Shared component PodTemplate with a pre-1.6 Planner | Valid; existing discovery contract |

For this DEP, conversion tests cover absent roles, complete roles, role-scoped provider overrides, and v1alpha1/v1beta1 round trips. Hash and lowering tests prove that the representation-only migration preserves the existing workload shape and rollout identity. The #12696 follow-up owns status tests for the serving-role projection across workload providers, v1alpha1/v1beta1 conversion, current-generation reads, and old-revision preservation during rolling updates.

### Alternatives

**Keep `multinode.leader` and `multinode.worker`.** This solves multinode locally but requires each compound component type to invent another structural API.

**Add only `multinode.worker.podTemplateOverrides`.** This is asymmetric and establishes user-visible merge semantics that do not naturally handle two complete heterogeneous PodTemplates.

**Allow partial role lists and infer missing roles.** This hides part of the desired structure and becomes ambiguous as role-level fields grow.

**Promote internal roles to sibling DGD components and group them.** This turns implementation fragments into graph nodes and moves the lifecycle boundary from the component to a group.

**Keep all roles implicit.** This cannot express the role-specific PodTemplates and provider configuration required by #12696 and future compound engines.

### Non-goals

This DEP does not define Component Group scaling, arbitrary subgraphs, graph-level workload programs, separate workload CRs, compiler ownership, SSA ownership of Grove resources, cross-resource transactions, KV-transfer wiring, TP/EP communication, Grove scheduling semantics, independent role autoscaling, or per-role public Services and status.

### Delivery

Completed roles foundation:

1. [#14419](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14419) (merged): add `roles[].name`, move the existing role-scoped `providerOverride`, preserve fixed multinode lowering, and support representation-only migration.
2. [#14477](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14477) (merged): add optional role cardinality while preserving `multinode.nodeCount` as the authoritative multinode shape.
3. [#14544](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14544) (merged): add the shared `roles[].podTemplate` API and deny-by-default capability check, without enabling role-template mode for a component.

Follow-up outside this DEP: [#12696](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/12696) owns complete multinode role PodTemplates, provider-neutral component status projection, and the Planner runtime gate. Its implementation [#14468](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14468) remains open.

### References

- [#12696: Add role-specific multinode PodTemplates and manual flag injection](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/12696)
- [#13253: implementation of split multinode worker overrides](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13253)
- [#13025: Scoped provider-native overrides for DGD workloads](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/13025)
- [#13273: provider-native workload override implementation](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13273)
- [#12699: Hierarchical component grouping and logical topology profiles](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/12699)
- [#12035: Decouple operator workload pathways from external orchestrators](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/12035)

title: DEP: LPX Component Type Integration
body:
> **Credit:** The design and implementation described in this DEP are the work of @andrewpaprotsky. I only collected the discussion and wrote it down here.

## Summary

Add `lpx` as a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) component type for deploying LPU-backed inference engines.

Unlike existing component types, an LPX component is lowered through an LPX-specific compiler. Starting from the component configuration, role-specific PodTemplates, and an immutable build, this compiler derives the complete LPU workload: LPU agent Pods and a conductor role materialized as either an LPU-only conductor or a GPU-side cyborg, together with runtime configuration, placement requests, and Grove topology.

The selected Grove workload program sends `type: lpx` components through this dedicated lowering path. LPX requires the Grove provider; the DCD workload program does not materialize LPX components. `LPXGraphDeployment` (LGD) is the generated Kubernetes object that persists the handoff to the LPX controller and exposes its status. It is an implementation boundary of the lowering path, not the main abstraction proposed by this DEP.

## Motivation

Dynamo component types already have type-specific semantics. A vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM component is not merely a PodTemplate: Dynamo interprets its engine type, topology, backend configuration, and role in the inference graph before producing Kubernetes workloads.

LPU-backed engines require another such lowering path. LPX is the compiler and runtime stack used to materialize them.

An LPX component describes a logical inference engine, but the resulting workload cannot be obtained by rendering its PodTemplate directly. Its immutable build and component roles must be processed by the LPX compiler to determine:

- a `conductor` role materialized as an LPU-only conductor or a hybrid GPU-side cyborg, according to the immutable build;
- the number and configuration of LPU `agent` roles;
- LPU partition and rank assignments;
- runtime configuration and commands;
- model preparation;
- scheduler placement intent;
- the resulting Grove `PodCliqueSet`, `PodCliqueScalingGroup`, and `PodClique` structure.

Adding this behavior as conditionals throughout the existing Grove renderer would make `type: lpx` a global mode of the DGD controller. The desired integration is another component lowering path selected through the workload-program architecture.

## Guiding principles

1. **A component type owns inference semantics.**

   The `roles` mechanism is shared across component types, but each component type defines the semantic role vocabulary and its interpretation. The LPX component implementation understands LPX builds, roles, compilation, runtime wiring, and readiness.

2. **Roles are semantic parts of a component.**

   LPX exposes `agent` for LPU execution and `conductor` for the coordinating role. The immutable build determines whether the conductor is materialized as an LPU-only Pod or a GPU-side cyborg. These remain roles inside one logical LPX engine component. They are not independent components reconstructed through a group.

3. **The Grove workload program selects the lowerer.**

   Every DGD component is claimed by exactly one materializer. Existing component types retain their current lowering.

4. **Groups are not semantic.**

   Scaling Groups, as explored separately in #14469, would provide an explicit outer scaling dimension and may optionally add a gang constraint. `component.replicas` and `scalingGroup.replicas` remain independent, multiplicative dimensions. Group membership must never change the meaning or validity of `component.replicas`, and groups must not encode what an LPX engine means.

5. **The selected lowerer owns its materialization details.**

   The DGD controller dispatches LPX intent and aggregates status. It does not interpret LPX compiler output or the resulting Grove child topology.

## Goals

- Support `type: lpx` as a DGD inference component type.
- Add a dedicated lowering path for LPU-backed components.
- Require the Grove workload provider for LPX components.
- Give the LPX lowering its own retryable and observable controller boundary.
- In the initial `v1alpha1`, allow one DGD-scoped LGD to claim all LPX components, including supported multi-component LPX workloads.
- Explicitly defer plural LGDs, component- or Scaling-Group-based claim partitioning, and claim transfer until Scaling Groups exist.
- Preserve DGD as the only user-authored API in the initial integration.
- Project LPX readiness and failures into ordinary DGD status.
- Keep deployments without LPX components on their existing reconciliation paths.
- Preserve a future path toward joint Grove graph assembly when explicitly required.

## Non-goals

- Making LGD a user-authored API in the initial version.
- Defining the final self-contained LGD specification.
- Introducing Component Groups or Scaling Groups.
- Creating multiple LGDs for one DGD in the initial integration.
- Partitioning LPX components into component- or Scaling-Group-scoped LGD claims in the initial integration.
- Defining claim-transfer or two-phase handoff semantics before plural LGDs and Scaling Groups exist.

- Allowing multiple controllers to modify the initial LPX-owned PCS.
- Providing Grove constraints across the ordinary and LPX PCS boundaries.
- Selecting Server-Side Apply or a render collector for future joint PCS assembly.
- Changing the behavior of non-LPX component types.

## Proposal

### LPX component shape

Users describe an LPX-backed engine as a normal DGD component:

```yaml
spec:
  components:
  - name: decode
    type: lpx
    replicas: 2

    lpx:
      buildId: model/build-abc

    roles:
    - name: conductor
      podTemplate:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: main
            image: lpu-conductor-runtime

    - name: agent
      podTemplate:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: main
            image: lpu-agent-runtime
```

The `roles` field is the shared DGD mechanism defined separately by #14417. It is encoded as a Kubernetes list-map keyed semantically by `name`. The mechanism is generic; its vocabulary is not. Each component type defines which role names are valid and what they mean during lowering. LPX uses `agent` and `conductor` for both LPU-only and hybrid engines. The build determines whether `conductor` becomes an LPU-only coordinator or a GPU-side cyborg.

> **Implementation status:** [PR #15062](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/15062) exposes the semantic `conductor` and `agent` roles. A hybrid build maps its `conductor` role to a GPU-side cyborg workload.

`component.replicas` remains the component-local multiplicity. Without an enclosing Scaling Group, the effective number of component instances equals `component.replicas`; with a future Scaling Group, it equals `scalingGroup.replicas × component.replicas`. Group membership must not change the field's meaning or validation. Exact role cardinalities and validation against the immutable build remain LPX lowering semantics; this DEP does not freeze them.

### Dedicated workload lowering

The selected Grove workload program partitions the graph according to component type:

```text
DynamoGraphDeployment
├── frontend, prefill, ... ──> existing lowerers
└── type: lpx ───────────────> LPX lowerer
```

The ordinary Grove lowerer ignores components claimed by LPX. The DCD workload program rejects LPX components because LPX requires Grove. Every component must be claimed exactly once. Deployments without LPX components remain unchanged.

Before Scaling Groups exist, all LPX components in one DGD form one implicit DGD-scoped materialization unit and are handed to one LGD. This is an initial compatibility rule, not the permanent composition model. The initial DGD reconciler is not required to model claim sets, partition LPX components, reconcile plural LGDs, or implement two-phase claim transfer. Those concerns are explicitly deferred to the Scaling Group follow-up.

### `LPXGraphDeployment` as persisted handoff

The DGD controller initially creates at most one LGD for a DGD. When LPX components exist, that LGD represents the implicit materialization unit containing all of them.

In the initial `v1alpha1`, the LGD spec contains only a controller-computed revision of the effective LPX inputs. Source identity is carried by an exact DGD controller `OwnerReference`, including the DGD name and UID. The initial singleton LGD may use the same namespace and name as its source DGD for lookup compatibility, but name equality is not the long-term identity contract and must not be required by the controller boundary. The LGD does not copy the DGD configuration:

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1alpha1
kind: LPXGraphDeployment
metadata:
  name: model
  namespace: default
  ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1beta1
    kind: DynamoGraphDeployment
    name: model
    uid: "<DGD UID>"
    controller: true
spec:
  inputRevision: sha256:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
```

The DGD controller calculates `inputRevision` from only the effective inputs to LPX lowering, including the selected restart token. In the initial singleton this means all LPX components. Once plural LGDs exist, each revision covers only the components and shared inputs of its claimed materialization unit. Changes outside that unit do not create a new LPX revision. The field is controller-populated rather than user-authored configuration.

The LGD controller validates that its controller `OwnerReference` exactly matches the source DGD identity, including API version, kind, name, and UID. It obtains the source DGD name from that owner reference rather than from the LGD name, extracts the claimed LPX components and relevant graph-level defaults, and reconciles the exact effective-input revision identified by `inputRevision`. Together, the exact owner identity, materialization-unit claim, and input revision provide the identity and fencing boundary for the handoff.

This intentionally avoids defining a second copy of the relevant DGD schema in the initial integration.

### Initial LGD and PCS identity

The initial integration creates at most one LGD per DGD. The singleton may use the source DGD name for lookup compatibility. Its exact DGD controller `OwnerReference`, including UID, remains the authoritative source identity.

The DGD controller selects and owns the LGD identity. The LGD controller selects and owns the PCS identity below that LGD and keeps the PCS identity private to its own reconciliation. No PCS name or reference is part of the DGD-to-LGD control contract. An optional status reference may be added later for a concrete observability or tooling use case, but DGD must not consume it and reconciliation correctness must not depend on it.

The owning LGD is the naming and reconciliation root for every resource it controls. PCS, runtime ConfigMaps, LPUPipelineRequests, endpoint resources, and other materialization children derive their names and reconciliation keys from the LGD or an explicit LGD-local materialization key, never from the source DGD name. The DGD name and component metadata may still be propagated through LGD PodTemplates onto Pods for discovery, observability, and user-facing attribution. Such labels are metadata, not lookup, ownership, fencing, or deletion authority. The LGD controller obtains source identity from the exact DGD controller OwnerReference.

### Materialization revision boundary

An LGD inputRevision defines one immutable materialization revision. Resources consumed by running Pods must not be changed in place from one revision to the next while the old workload can still run. Runtime ConfigMaps are therefore revision-specific snapshots whose names are rooted in the LGD identity and include a bounded input-revision or content digest. The controller creates the successor resources, references them only from the successor PCS, retains the previous resources while the previous PCS exists, and garbage-collects them after retirement.

Recovery and other destructive actions establish authority through the concrete LGD-owned Kubernetes object chain. For Grove Pods this means validating the owner chain from Pod through PodClique, PodCliqueScalingGroup, and PodCliqueSet to the exact LGD name and UID. Revision annotations may provide additional fencing, but source-DGD labels never substitute for ownership.

### Future: plural LGDs and claim handoff

> This section records follow-up constraints for the Scaling Group design. It is not an implementation requirement for the initial LPX integration.

Once Scaling Groups and plural LGD reconciliation exist, the durable identity of an LGD is expected to be its source DGD plus a materialization-unit key:

```text
(DGD UID, component, <component name>)
or
(DGD UID, scaling-group, <group name>)
```

The future DGD controller would own the desired set of LGD claims and allocate a stable, collision-resistant LGD name from that key. LGD naming must not depend on a compiled Grove graph or PCS name.

Changing the future partition from one unit to another is an ownership transfer. To prevent two active LGDs from materializing the same component, that design will need a fenced handoff, conceptually:

1. **Prepare:** allocate or update the desired LGD identities and revisions without giving a new LGD overlapping materialization authority.
2. **Commit:** activate the new claim only after any predecessor LGD that claimed the same component has fenced and retired its workload.

The exact future claim API, naming scheme, and handoff protocol belong to the Scaling Group follow-up. They are deliberately not selected by this DEP and need not be implemented by the initial PR.

### LPX lowering responsibilities

The LPX controller performs the complete type-specific lowering:

```text
LPX component intent
        │
        ▼
resolve immutable build
        │
        ▼
prepare model artifacts
        │
        ▼
compile roles and LPU topology
        │
        ▼
render runtime configuration
        │
        ▼
create LPUPipelineRequest and Grove workload
        │
        ▼
observe placement, readiness, and recovery
```

It owns the resulting LPX-specific resources and behavior, including:

- runtime `ConfigMap` and `Service` objects;
- `LPUPipelineRequest`;
- the LPX `PodCliqueSet`;
- scheduler and placement interaction;
- retry, fencing, recovery, and cleanup;
- detailed LPX status.

The DGD controller owns workload selection, LGD creation, ordinary component lowering, aggregate status, and deletion ordering. It must not reproduce the LPX state machine or depend on the names of LPX Grove children.

### Initial singleton and future materialization-unit partitioning

LGD is a deployment and materialization boundary, not a compiler artifact. Each LPX component references its own immutable compiler artifact through `buildId`.

Before Scaling Groups exist, the initial integration has exactly zero or one LGD per DGD. If LPX components exist, the single LGD claims all of them. It supports either multiple independent complete LPX engines, each with its own `conductor` and `agent` roles, or one shared uniform speculative-decoding draft/target pair. A shared pair cannot be mixed with additional independent LPX engines. The shared pair lowers as:

```text
DGD
├── frontend
├── draft   type: lpx, buildId: draft/build-abc ─┐
└── target  type: lpx, buildId: target/build-def ┴──> implicit all-LPX unit
                                                        └──> one LGD
                                                             └──> one coupled LPX Grove workload
```

The compiler artifacts remain distinct, while LPX lowers them into one coupled SpecDecode workload. In the current implementation, target component replicas are restricted to one; draft component replicas express draft multiplicity and are unfolded into distinct Agent clique templates inside one LPX PCSG whose replica count is also one. This is a type-specific restriction, not a rule conditional on group membership.

For independent complete engines, the same LGD claims every LPX component and owns one LPX PCS containing a separate workload group for each engine. Sharing that initial LGD and PCS is a materialization choice; the engines remain distinct DGD components with independent serving semantics and component replica counts. This initial all-LPX claim does not define the future partition.

The implicit all-LPX unit is the complete scope of the initial integration. Plural LGDs and component- or group-based partitioning are a follow-up that starts only once Scaling Groups exist. The expected future partition is:

```text
ungrouped LPX component                  -> one LGD for that component
LPX components in the same Scaling Group -> one LGD for that group
```

Two ungrouped LPX components therefore produce two LGDs. They may still participate in speculative-decoding wiring, but they do not gain one materialization, scaling, or gang boundary merely because both have `type: lpx`. If they require one shared LPX materialization and Grove scheduling scope, an explicit Scaling Group supplies that boundary.

The Scaling Group does not define speculative-decoding semantics and does not combine compiler artifacts. LPX component and wiring logic still decides whether the claimed component set is a valid SpecDecode shape and how its separate builds interact. The group only establishes the shared materialization unit, outer replica dimension, and optional gang constraint.

### Status projection

LGD exposes rich status from the initial version, including:

- observed source input;
- compilation and placement state;
- model-preparation state;
- readiness for each claimed DGD component;
- retry, recovery, and terminal failures;

The DGD controller projects this into normal component status and computes aggregate DGD readiness. Users continue to observe the DGD as the primary resource.

### Future self-contained LGD spec

A future API revision may make LGD independently reconcilable by copying the relevant part of the DGD into its spec. This would make LGD effectively a filtered DGD.

The following sketch is illustrative. It shows the expected shape and data ownership, but does not propose final field names, nesting, or another API version:

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.com/<future-version>
kind: LPXGraphDeployment
metadata:
  name: model-lpx
spec:
  inputRevision: sha256:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef

  # Illustrative future selector; exact field names are not proposed here.
  materializationUnit:
    scalingGroup: specdecode

  scheduling: ...
  labels:
    example: value
  annotations:
    example: value
  env:
  - name: EXAMPLE
    value: value
  priorityClassName: high-priority
  backendFramework: ...

  components:
  - name: draft
    type: lpx
    replicas: 2
    lpx:
      buildId: draft/build-abc
    roles:
    - name: agent
      podTemplate: ...

  - name: target
    type: lpx
    replicas: 1
    lpx:
      buildId: target/build-def
    roles:
    - name: conductor
      podTemplate: ...
    - name: agent
      podTemplate: ...
```

The illustrative `materializationUnit` identifies the subset claimed from the owning DGD. A single ungrouped engine would instead identify `component: decode`. It is not another reference to the source DGD; source identity remains the exact controller `OwnerReference`. The field name and union encoding are intentionally not fixed here.

This illustrative speculative-decoding shape is LPU-only, so the target's `conductor` materializes as an LPU-only Pod. A separately supported hybrid engine also uses the `conductor` role, materialized as a GPU-side cyborg; this example does not imply hybrid SpecDecode support. The component replica values remain local multiplicities; the selected Scaling Group supplies the independent outer multiplier.

The two `buildId` values deliberately remain separate compiler artifacts. Their pairing and shared materialization are LPX lowering semantics, not evidence of a combined compiler artifact.

The exact DGD controller `OwnerReference` remains the ownership and source-identity boundary, while the copied LGD spec becomes the authoritative reconciliation input. Until that future API is defined, the initial `v1alpha1` contains only `inputRevision`; the initial LGD implicitly claims all LPX components and reads their effective inputs from the DGD named by its controller owner reference.

Only actual LPX inputs should be copied. LGD should not become a second complete DGD API.

### Initial Grove materialization

The initial integration uses separate Grove objects:

```text
existing DGD lowering             LPX lowering
         │                             │
         ▼                             ▼
PodCliqueSet / normal          PodCliqueSet / lpx
owner: DGD                     owner: LGD
```

This provides unambiguous writer, retry, finalizer, and deletion ownership.

Runtime traffic may cross the boundary through Dynamo discovery and services. Grove-native constraints cannot initially cross it, including colocation, `startsAfter`, shared PCSG indices, or one Grove rollout envelope.

#### Initial implementation assumption: Grove naming and addressing

The initial LPX lowerer follows the same compatibility boundary as today's multi-node Grove lowering. It may render peer addresses from Grove-injected environment variables and Grove's published name-generation helpers. For example, current multi-node rendering configures a leader address with a form equivalent to:

```text
$(GROVE_PCSG_NAME)-$(GROVE_PCSG_INDEX)-<component>-ldr-0.$(GROVE_HEADLESS_SERVICE)
```

The controller constructs this expression; the Pod only expands the environment variables injected by Grove. The assumption is therefore not that generated names are opaque. It is that their shape is a published, versioned Grove API contract. A breaking change in that contract is a compatibility risk already shared by multi-node components; LPX does not introduce a new category of coupling here.

This does not permit the DGD controller to select, reconstruct, or watch LGD-owned Grove child names. In particular, the DGD-to-LGD handoff selects the LGD identity, not its PCS name. The LPX controller chooses, owns, and privately reconciles the PCS identity and may use Grove's published contract while materializing and wiring descendants. Neither controller should duplicate undocumented Grove naming rules or introduce LPX-specific naming conventions. A future Grove API may provide explicit sibling references or addresses and remove descendant-name reconstruction for both multi-node and LPX, but that is not required by this DEP.

### Future joint Grove materialization

Separate PCSs are not necessarily a permanent restriction.

DEP #14420 describes how independent workload lowerers could eventually contribute to one joint PCS when an explicit Grove-level constraint requires it. Possible mechanisms include:

- multi-writer Server-Side Apply with disjoint field managers; or
- a Grove render collector acting as the sole PCS writer.

This DEP does not select or implement either mechanism. The initial LPX integration must merely preserve the prerequisites identified by #14420: stable contribution identities, explicit references, collision-free keys, generation-aware results, singular deletion authority, and no dependency on undocumented or LPX-specific Grove naming rules.

### Scaling Groups

Scaling Groups are explored separately in #14469 and are outside the initial LPX integration.

A Scaling Group introduces an outer replica dimension without changing the meaning of any member component. Its replica count composes multiplicatively with each member's component-local replica count:

```text
effective component instances
    = scalingGroup.replicas × component.replicas
```

Without an enclosing Scaling Group, the outer multiplier is implicitly one. For example:

```yaml
components:
- name: draft
  type: lpx
  replicas: 2
- name: target
  type: lpx
  replicas: 1

experimental:
  scalingGroups:
  - name: specdec
    replicas: 10
    components:
    - draft
    - target
```

This describes twenty draft instances and ten target instances. The outer Grove PCSG replica count is ten, derived exclusively from `scalingGroup.replicas`. The component-local multiplicities are represented inside each group replica, through deterministic unfolding or a future nested Grove graph representation. Role-level Pod cardinalities remain a separate component-type concern and may, as for LPX Agents, be derived from an immutable build.

Membership in a Scaling Group must never make an otherwise valid `component.replicas` value invalid, or make an otherwise invalid value valid. An LPX component type may impose an unconditional replica restriction, but it cannot make that restriction depend on group membership.

Once plural LGDs are supported, a Scaling Group may additionally select one shared LGD materialization boundary for its LPX members; ungrouped LPX components receive separate LGDs. This follows from the requested shared scaling and scheduling scope and does not make the group semantic.

The boundary between both concepts is intentional: LPX component and wiring logic supplies component-type and SpecDecode semantics, while a Scaling Group provides a materialization boundary, outer scaling dimension, and optional gang coupling for otherwise independently meaningful components. It must not provide LPX compiler semantics or reconstruct one LPX engine from fragments that cannot exist independently.

## Alternate solutions

### Add LPX conditionals to the existing Grove renderer

This can produce the required objects, but turns LPX into a cross-cutting DGD mode and mixes two substantially different lowering processes.

### Expose conductor and agents as sibling components

This makes compiler-generated LPX roles appear independently meaningful and requires another API object to reconstruct the engine. Role-aware components preserve the logical engine boundary.

### Always create one LGD per LPX component

This is not sufficient as a universal rule. It is the future default for ungrouped LPX components, but an explicit Scaling Group may require several LPX components to share one LGD, one outer replica dimension, and one Grove scheduling scope.

The initial implementation temporarily chooses the opposite fallback—one LGD for all LPX components—because claim partitioning and plural LGDs are deferred. This includes multiple independent complete engines as well as a shared uniform SpecDecode pair. Neither fallback is the permanent model. The materialization-unit partition determines LGD cardinality.

### Route every LPX component through a DCD

A DCD represents one component lifecycle. An LGD may claim several components within one materialization boundary, whether they form a coupled SpecDecode workload or remain independent engines, so a single DCD is not its natural ownership boundary. Grove workload programs may also already materialize selected graph subsets without a DCD per component.

### Define a complete standalone LGD API immediately

This remains a possible follow-up. Doing it initially would stabilize the copied DGD surface before its actual dependency boundary is understood.

### Produce one shared PCS immediately

Deferred, not rejected. #14420 keeps both SSA and collector-based assembly available when an explicit cross-boundary Grove constraint requires it.

## Requirements

### Initial integration requirements

1. DGD accepts `type: lpx` as an inference component type.
2. The selected Grove workload program assigns every component to exactly one lowerer; LPX requires Grove.
3. The ordinary Grove lowerer ignores components claimed by LPX; the DCD workload program rejects LPX.
4. Deployments without LPX components retain their current behavior.
5. The `roles` mechanism is shared across component types, while each component type owns its semantic role vocabulary and interpretation. LPX accepts `agent` and `conductor`; the build determines whether the conductor materializes as an LPU-only Pod or a GPU-side cyborg.
6. Before Scaling Groups exist, a DGD has at most one LGD, and that LGD claims all LPX components in the DGD.
7. Initial multi-component LPX claims may contain multiple independent complete engines or one shared uniform SpecDecode draft/target pair. The pair retains separate compiler artifacts and cannot be mixed with additional independent LPX engines.
8. The LGD uses an exact DGD controller `OwnerReference`, including UID, as its source identity.
9. The singleton LGD may use the DGD name initially, but source validation and lookup use the exact controller owner identity rather than treating name equality as ownership.
10. `inputRevision` covers the effective inputs of all LPX components in the initial singleton, including the selected restart token; unrelated non-LPX changes do not create its revision.
11. The DGD controller selects the LGD identity but does not assign or infer its PCS name.
12. The LPX controller selects, owns, and privately reconciles the LPX PCS identity. No PCS name or reference is required by or consumed by the DGD controller.
13. Every LGD-owned child name and reconciliation key is rooted in the LGD or an explicit LGD-local materialization key, never in the source DGD name.
14. DGD and component labels may be propagated through LGD PodTemplates for discovery and attribution, but the LPX controller must not use them as lookup, ownership, fencing, or deletion authority.
15. Runtime configuration and other revision-sensitive resources consumed by Pods are immutable per-LGD-revision snapshots. A successor revision must not update resources still consumed by the retiring workload.
16. Recovery and eviction validate the exact LGD-owned Kubernetes owner chain and revision before mutating workload children.
17. The LPX controller owns LPX compilation, resources, retries, recovery, and status.
18. DGD projects LGD results into normal component and aggregate status.
19. The LPX lowerer may use Grove's published, versioned identity and addressing contract, as existing multi-node lowering does, but must not duplicate undocumented rules or introduce LPX-specific naming conventions.
20. The initial integration uses exclusive PCS ownership.
21. Scaling Groups, plural LGDs, component- or group-based claim partitioning, and two-phase claim transfer are not initial requirements; they are deferred to #14469 and its follow-up implementation.
22. The design preserves the future joint-PCS options described by #14420.

### Scaling Group follow-up invariants

These constraints apply when Scaling Groups and plural LGD reconciliation are designed. They do not expand the scope of the initial LPX PR.

1. Future plural reconciliation creates one LGD per ungrouped LPX component and one LGD per Scaling Group claimed by LPX.
2. A Scaling Group establishes a shared materialization boundary, outer replica dimension, and optional gang constraint. It does not define LPX or SpecDecode semantics.
3. Every LPX component belongs to exactly one desired materialization-unit claim and at most one active LGD.
4. LGD identity is derived from the exact source DGD identity and a stable component- or Scaling-Group-based materialization-unit key, not from a compiled Grove graph or PCS name.
5. A materialization-unit repartition uses a fenced handoff; a successor LGD cannot materialize a component until its predecessor has retired that claim.
6. Each LGD's `inputRevision` covers only the effective inputs of its claimed materialization unit.
7. `component.replicas` and `scalingGroup.replicas` are independent, multiplicative dimensions; group membership must not change component replica semantics or validation.
8. For grouped components, the outer PCS or PCSG replica count comes from the Scaling Group dimension. Member component multiplicities are represented within each group replica through unfolding or hierarchy.

## References

- #14417
- #14469
- #14420
- #12035
- #12625
- [Internal LPX design document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-sDqwqVVD2EJyJ8y6TeqFKBNOc7uNf9C8-N_l0j7kQs/edit?usp=sharing)

title: DEP: North Star: Make DGD workload materialization and logical wiring orthogonal
body:
## Summary

Define two orthogonal composition axes as the architectural north star for `DynamoGraphDeployment` reconciliation:

1. **Workload materialization** decides which controller and Kubernetes resource realize each component, for example a `DynamoComponentDeployment`, direct Grove lowering, a `DisaggregatedSet`, a future Elastic EP `EnginePool`, or an `LPXGraphDeployment`.
2. **Logical wiring** decides how components and their internal roles communicate, for example request routing, KV exchange, speculative decoding, or leader/worker rendezvous for tensor and expert parallelism.

One selected graph-level workload program continues to own the complete DGD reconciliation state machine. Inside that program, focused reconcilers may claim disjoint component subsets and materialize them through different workload resources. Wiring is compiled from semantic component identities, capabilities, roles, and stable endpoint declarations rather than from the concrete resource kind that happened to deploy a component.

This separation allows either axis to evolve independently: a component can move from direct Grove lowering to an independently reconciled workload resource without redesigning its communication contract, and a new wiring pattern can connect components without teaching it whether they are backed by a DCD, EnginePool, LPXGraphDeployment, or another provider object.

![DGD north star: workload materialization and logical wiring as orthogonal axes](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3b1d2cf2-3d95-4d0a-ab68-8b128fea23bc)

## Motivation

Dynamo already has heterogeneous workload materialization at several levels:

- A multinode worker component lowers to distinct Leader and Worker Pods.
- The component pathway creates one `DynamoComponentDeployment` per DGD component, and each DCD may lower to a `Deployment` or `LeaderWorkerSet`.
- The Grove pathway lowers one DGD into PodCliqueSet resources, including PodCliqueScalingGroups for compound components.
- The DisaggregatedSet pathway selects several eligible worker components as roles of one `DisaggregatedSet` while lowering the remaining components to DCDs.

These shapes demonstrate that one DGD program may already own several child kinds. Future integrations increase that pressure: Elastic EP may justify an `EnginePool` lifecycle boundary, while a compiled multi-role engine may justify an `LPXGraphDeployment`. [nvidia-lpu/lpu-dynamo#414](https://github.com/nvidia-lpu/lpu-dynamo/pull/414) explores the latter persisted boundary and currently aggregates the selected LPX components into one private child. This DEP does not standardize that cardinality: a materializer must explicitly claim its component set, and the program must support multiple child instances when the semantic and lifecycle boundaries require them. These objects can be correct retry, ownership, compilation, rollout, or observability boundaries without becoming new graph programs.

First, a graph program may need more than one kind of persisted child resource. A specialized controller can own one component's internal lifecycle while ordinary components continue through the existing DCD or Grove lowering. A single DGD may contain multiple such specialized components. Creating a new graph program for every specialized component type is not sufficient: mixed graphs still need one owner for finalization, ordering, restart, rollout, stable resources, readiness aggregation, and DGD status.

The physical decomposition must not determine logical communication. A prefill and decode pair still needs the same KV-transfer intent whether one side is a DCD, a direct Grove contribution, or a specialized child CR. A multinode leader and its workers still need rendezvous and rank identity whether they become a LeaderWorkerSet, Grove PodCliques, or an EnginePool. The implementation may differ in how a stable endpoint becomes a Service name, headless DNS name, Pod ordinal, or runtime environment variable, but those addressing adapters must not redefine the semantic edge.

Conversely, communication must not determine materialization. A speculative-decoding drafter and verifier may both use one materializer, different materializers, or two instances of the same specialized child type. That should not require a new graph-level program for each combination.

Issue #12035 established composition-first reconciliation programs: one complete program owns control flow and reuses smaller building blocks with genuinely shared invariants. PR #12625 demonstrates that one such program can own heterogeneous child kinds without invoking another complete program. DEP #14417 defines inward component roles for compound components. This DEP defines the larger DGD structure in which materializers, role-aware renderers, and logical wiring are composed.

## Goals

- Keep exactly one graph-level workload program selected for a DGD.
- Allow a program to compose concrete reconcilers for disjoint component subsets.
- Establish workload materialization and logical wiring as independent DGD architecture axes.
- Support zero, one, or multiple specialized child deployments of each kind in one DGD.
- Allow future materialization boundaries such as `EnginePool` and `LPXGraphDeployment` without creating a graph program per component kind.
- Compile inter-component and intra-component communication from semantic identities and endpoint contracts rather than concrete workload kinds.
- Make the unavoidable address-formation adapter explicit and narrow.
- Keep the selected program as the sole writer of aggregate DGD workload status.
- Preserve the component as the inference-aware lifecycle and scaling unit, as defined further by DEP #14417.
- Reuse normalization, PodTemplate rendering, stable-resource reconciliation, and status helpers where their invariants are shared.
- Keep provider-specific object models, naming, watches, readiness, rollout, and cleanup semantics in focused reconcilers.
- Make duplicate, missing, or stale component ownership detectable and testable.
- Permit a future joint Grove PodCliqueSet to be assembled from independently reconciled component contributions without making every child controller understand the whole graph.

## Non-goals

- A universal provider callback framework or common provider state machine.
- Calling one complete workload program from another workload program.
- Redefining the component-role API proposed by DEP #14417.
- Treating component roles as arbitrary user-defined graph topology.
- Exposing Grove PodClique, PodCliqueScalingGroup, or object-naming concepts in semantic DGD APIs.
- Replacing `DynamoComponentDeployment`, Grove, LeaderWorkerSet, or DisaggregatedSet.
- Selecting server-side apply or a Grove render collector as the final joint-PCS assembly mechanism in the initial refactor.
- Promising cross-child atomic rollout or colocation merely because contributions can be assembled into one object.
- Changing the durable workload-provider selection mechanism.
- Migrating existing DGDs between workload providers.

## Proposal

### 1. DGD north star: two orthogonal axes

The DGD architecture treats physical materialization and logical communication as independent dimensions:

| Workload materializer | Standalone request | KV exchange | Speculative decoding | TP/EP rendezvous |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DCD / Deployment / LWS | possible | possible | possible | possible |
| Direct Grove lowering | possible | possible | possible | possible |
| DisaggregatedSet | possible | possible | possible | possible |
| EnginePool | future | future | future | primary use case |
| LPXGraphDeployment | future | future | primary use case | primary use case |

Not every cell must be implemented, but neither axis defines the other. A materializer realizes its claimed set of one or more components; a wiring compiler connects semantic endpoints. The narrow bridge between them is an explicit endpoint and runtime-binding contract.

```text
DynamoGraphDeployment
    |
    +- semantic components, roles, capabilities and graph relationships
    |
    +- MATERIALIZATION
    |    |- direct Grove contributor
    |    |- DynamoComponentDeployment
    |    |- DisaggregatedSet
    |    |- EnginePool                         (future)
    |    `- LPXGraphDeployment                 (future)
    |
    `- WIRING
         |- request/service edge
         |- KV-transfer edge
         |- speculative draft/verify edge
         `- leader/worker or agent rendezvous
```

One selected `workloadProgram` owns the complete graph reconcile and orders both axes. A graph program may contain many focused reconcilers. "Complete program" means that the program owns graph-level control flow and status; it does not mean that the implementation is monolithic or that every component uses the same child resource.

Programs do not invoke other complete programs:

```text
incorrect: groveProgram -> componentProgram -> anotherProgram

correct:   groveProgram
             |- componentClassifier
             |- endpointDeclarationReconciler
             |- logicalWiringCompiler
             |- ordinaryGroveMaterializer
             |- enginePoolChildrenReconciler
             |- lpxGraphDeploymentChildrenReconciler
             |- groveAssemblyReconciler
             |- scalingAdaptersReconciler
             `- aggregate status projection
```

These are concrete collaborators inside one program, not provider callbacks in a universal lifecycle framework.

### 2. Declare, wire, then materialize

Wiring cannot be an afterthought applied only after Pods exist: workload commands, environment variables and ConfigMaps may require peer addresses during rendering. Materialization also cannot own all wiring, because the peer may be realized by another controller and resource kind.

The program therefore uses a staged contract:

```text
1. normalize DGD component and role intent
2. classify each component and assign exactly one materializer
3. declare stable logical endpoints and workload identities
4. compile graph and role relationships into runtime bindings
5. reconcile stable Services, ConfigMaps and other binding resources
6. pass bindings into each materializer or its child CR
7. obtain direct resources or asynchronously published render contributions
8. assemble and reconcile provider-native workloads
9. observe child/provider status and project aggregate DGD status
```

Endpoint declaration precedes physical workload creation. A declaration can resolve deterministically to a Service reference, role identity or provider-neutral endpoint handle without requiring a live Pod. If an external controller determines an endpoint dynamically, it publishes an observed-generation-guarded endpoint result and the graph program requeues until it is available.

The order is a program concern. It is not a requirement that every collaborator implement one common `Render/Ready/Rollout` interface.

### 3. Component claiming inside a program

Component normalization occurs once per graph reconcile. The selected program then assigns every normalized component to exactly one workload contributor.

The initial implementation should use concrete reconcilers rather than a universal provider interface. A small internal value may make ownership and aggregation explicit:

```go
type ComponentClaim struct {
    ComponentName string
    Contributor   string
}

type WorkloadContribution struct {
    Resources  []Resource
    Components map[string]v1beta1.ComponentReplicaStatus
    Conditions []metav1.Condition
}
```

The program is responsible for validating that:

- every component is claimed exactly once;
- two contributors do not claim the same component;
- returned component status belongs to a claimed component;
- stale children from an earlier set of claims are removed safely; and
- a contributor failure is projected through the program's native error and status policy.

This is a mechanical composition contract, not a claim that contributors share rollout, readiness, revision, or scaling semantics.

### 4. Concrete program composition

The existing graph programs retain their complete state machines and compose focused workload reconcilers.

#### ComponentProgram

```text
componentProgram
    |- common graph resources
    |- component workload reconciliation
    |    `- zero or more DynamoComponentDeployments
    |- rollout and scaling adapters
    `- DCD status aggregation
```

The DCD controller remains the persisted retry and ownership boundary that lowers one component to a `Deployment` or `LeaderWorkerSet`.

#### GroveProgram

```text
groveProgram
    |- common graph resources
    |- ordinary Grove workload reconciler
    |    `- components handled directly by Grove lowering
    |- specialized child-deployment reconciler
    |    `- zero or more child CRs for claimed materialization units
    |- Grove-specific rollout, scaling, topology, and readiness
    `- aggregate component status
```

The specialized child reconciler is set-oriented. It deterministically reconciles one child per claimed materialization unit, which may contain one or several components, deletes stale owned children, and returns current status for every claimed component. Each child controller owns its provider-specific compilation and workload lifecycle.

This supports graphs containing two or more specialized components without selecting multiple graph programs.

#### DisaggregatedProgram

```text
disaggregatedSetProgram
    |- common graph resources
    |- selected eligible worker components
    |    `- one DisaggregatedSet with embedded role LeaderWorkerSetSpecs
    |- remaining components
    |    `- zero or more DynamoComponentDeployments
    `- aggregate DisaggregatedSet and DCD readiness
```

DisaggregatedSet roles are graph-level roles whose members are complete DGD components. They are distinct from the component-internal roles defined by DEP #14417.

### 5. Component-internal roles

[DEP #14417](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/14417) defines the public component-role API. This DEP consumes its result rather than reopening its API decisions.

A role refines the inside of one semantic component. It does not become a DGD graph node or an independently owned workload component. The graph program resolves the component and its roles into a provider-neutral model before either materialization or wiring:

```go
type ResolvedComponent struct {
    Name     string
    Type     v1beta1.ComponentType
    Replicas int32
    Roles    []ResolvedRole
}

type ResolvedRole struct {
    Name        string
    Replicas    int32
    PodTemplate corev1.PodTemplateSpec
    Endpoints   []EndpointDeclaration
}
```

`ResolvedRole` contains semantic role information, effective PodTemplates and semantic endpoint declarations. It must not contain Grove, LeaderWorkerSet, DisaggregatedSet, scheduler, or provider-generated object names.

For example, the resolved `leader` and `worker` roles of a multinode engine can participate in a rendezvous binding while still materializing through either LeaderWorkerSet or Grove. A specialized compiled engine can resolve coordinator and agent roles and then delegate their physical realization to an `LPXGraphDeployment`.

### 6. Workload materializers

Each workload implementation translates the same resolved component roles into its native objects:

| Semantic component shape | Possible materialization |
| --- | --- |
| Single-Pod engine or frontend | DCD -> Deployment, or direct Grove PodClique |
| Multinode leader + workers | DCD -> LeaderWorkerSet, direct Grove PCSG, or future EnginePool |
| Disaggregated component set | DisaggregatedSet plus DCDs for the remaining graph |
| Elastic expert-parallel engine | direct Grove initially; future EnginePool child boundary |
| Specialized compiled multi-role engine | LPXGraphDeployment -> provider-native workloads |

The table is deliberately many-to-many. A semantic shape does not permanently select a Kubernetes resource kind, and a materializer is not a communication mode.

Concrete materializers remain responsible for their child API, watches, compilation, rollout interpretation, readiness, cleanup and native resource naming. They consume resolved components and runtime bindings. They must not rediscover DGD relationships by inspecting sibling workload object names.

The initial implementation can keep direct Grove lowering in-process. A persisted child such as `EnginePool` or `LPXGraphDeployment` is introduced only when it provides an independent retry, ownership, compilation, rollout, scaling or observability boundary.

### 7. Multiple specialized components

A specialized child deployment is scoped to a materialization unit rather than necessarily to one component. A unit may claim one component or several complete components when its materializer supports their shared lifecycle. Its identity is derived from the owning DGD and a stable unit key; source identity includes the exact DGD UID. The claimed component set may be explicit or, for the initial LPX singleton, implicit in the DGD-scoped handoff. The graph program must still assign each component to exactly one active materializer claim.

```text
DGD
    |- ordinary component A -> ordinary provider workload
    |- specialized component B -+
    `- specialized component C -+-> one shared child deployment
```

The graph program owns the collection of children. Each child controller owns only its claimed components' materialization and native workload resources. The graph program aggregates status for each claimed component together with ordinary component status.

Relationships between specialized components, such as speculative draft and verifier request flow, remain semantic wiring. They do not by themselves determine child cardinality. Two components may be claimed by one child when the materializer supports a shared unit, or by separate children when their lifecycle boundaries are independent. In the initial LPX integration, one DGD-scoped LGD claims all LPX components, including multiple independent engines; #14473 defines that compatibility boundary and its future partitioning.

### 8. Logical wiring

Logical wiring describes why two semantic endpoints communicate, not which Kubernetes resources contain their Pods. It includes both inter-component and intra-component relationships:

| Wiring intent | Example producer and consumer | Materialization-independent meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request/service | frontend -> engine | Send inference requests to a ready component endpoint |
| KV transfer | prefill -> decode | Transfer KV state using the selected transport and endpoint capabilities |
| Speculative decoding | verifier/target -> drafter | Bind the verifier to one or more draft endpoints |
| Rendezvous | leader -> workers | Form one distributed engine instance with rank and leader identity |
| Expert-parallel membership | coordinator -> ranks | Join the same EP control and data plane |

Some relationships are inferred today from component types and backend configuration rather than expressed as explicit DGD edges. This DEP does not require a new graph-edge API. It requires the reconciler to normalize those existing semantics into a wiring model before provider-specific rendering.

Conceptually:

```go
type EndpointRef struct {
    ComponentName string
    RoleName      string // optional
    Port          string
    Protocol      string
}

type WiringIntent struct {
    Kind     WiringKind
    Consumer EndpointRef
    Producer EndpointRef
    Policy   WiringPolicy
}

type RuntimeBinding struct {
    Consumer EndpointRef
    Values   []BindingValue // service refs, env, args, config or typed handles
}
```

These are illustrative internal values, not a proposed public API. `WiringIntent` must not contain DCD, EnginePool, LPXGraphDeployment, PodClique or PodCliqueScalingGroup names.

The wiring compiler consumes semantic relationships and endpoint declarations. A materialization adapter translates the resulting binding into the concrete form required by its workload: a stable Service DNS name, a headless Service, an ordinal-aware hostname, environment variables, command arguments, a ConfigMap entry, or a child-CR reference.

The invariant is:

```text
wire(A, B, kind) depends on A/B capabilities and EndpointRefs,
not on whether A or B is deployed by DCD, Grove, EnginePool or LPXGraphDeployment.
```

Address formation is the explicit exception. The adapter may need to know how the selected materializer publishes or derives an endpoint, but that knowledge is confined to endpoint resolution and does not leak into graph semantics.

### 9. Endpoint and binding contract

Every materializer declares the endpoints and identities it can provide before workload rendering. A declaration uses stable semantic keys:

```go
type EndpointDeclaration struct {
    Ref          EndpointRef
    Scope        EndpointScope // component, role, replica or rank
    AddressClass AddressClass  // service, headless, ordinal, runtime-published
    Capabilities []Capability
}

type ComponentMaterialization struct {
    ComponentName string
    Materializer  string
    ChildRef      *corev1.ObjectReference
    Endpoints     []EndpointDeclaration
}
```

The concrete representation may be an ephemeral program value, a child spec, or observed child status depending on the ownership boundary. The contract must preserve these properties:

- endpoint identity is stable across rollout revisions;
- the producer of an endpoint owns its address realization;
- consumers refer to semantic endpoint identity, not inferred object names;
- status-derived endpoints carry source generation and freshness;
- a child can publish explicit references without exposing how it factors its internal Grove resources;
- missing or stale endpoint information blocks only the dependent binding and is reported through the program's status policy.

Internal role wiring follows the same rule. A multinode renderer may resolve the leader endpoint into LWS-specific or Grove-specific DNS, while an EnginePool may publish its own rendezvous handle. The engine's leader/worker relationship remains the same semantic input.

### 10. Composing one Grove graph from decomposed workloads

![Three ways to assemble one Grove PodCliqueSet from decomposed workload controllers](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/725465bb-c2e4-4213-9988-20ae71f1ab14)
